exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw a ring buffer or free list as an actual circle with Head/Tail arrows and a null slot rather than a generic queue box, chain each table entry to its resource with a dashed indirection arrow, and number the steps so they cross the host/device boundary through explicit NIC boxes on both sides.

exemplars.why_chosen: An explicit boxed legend maps dashed to the management path and solid to the data path, separating the dashed host-side transport region above from the solid NIC hardware (TX Merge, RX Split, Flow Table) below.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Put a small boxed legend that names dashed as the management path and solid as the data path, then honor it everywhere: dashed for the host-side software containers, solid for the on-chip hardware, and color the two traffic directions (blue send, red receive) only where they physically cross at the net port.

exemplars.why_chosen: Medium-confidence top-down variant: three vertical colored paths (Outbound blue, Inbound-Fast solid red, Inbound-Slow dashed red) run through both sides of an explicit PCIe boundary, making solid-vs-dashed red read directly as hardware-vs-software retransmission.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Run each named path, labeled inline at the top instead of a legend box, as one vertical colored line from the software layer through the PCIe boundary into the matching hardware block, and use solid versus dashed on the same color to split a fast hardware path from its slow software fallback.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated: matching section-number tags and identical blue fill tie the compute blade's cache controller directly to the switch's cache directory across the split, though the switch's own Control Plane band is left unlabeled inside.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Tag two mechanisms that must be read together, one on the host side and one on the device side, with the same paper-section number and fill color so the eye links them without an arrow; don't leave a named band like Control Plane empty, or its role stays implicit as it does here.

exemplars.why_chosen: A software instance of the template: per-host Mint-agent/collector components connect via numbered, colored arrows to a separate Mint-backend, with a below-figure icon legend decoding the common-pattern, variable-parameter, and bloom-filter glyphs used on both sides.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Host-device does not require hardware: split a per-host agent from its backend service the same way, reuse one small icon set (pattern/parameter/metadata glyphs) on both sides so the legend only has to be defined once, and color the arrows by what they always report versus what they only report when sampled.

exemplars.why_chosen: Simple, single-flow host-device figure: shadow-stacked host boxes (implying N repeated hosts) sit symmetrically against one CXL memory-node box, joined by a single CXL Links arrow, though neither the host count nor request-vs-response direction is labeled.
exemplars.what_to_learn: A shadow-stacked box implies repetition even at nesting depth 2 with no lanes, but unlike this figure, label the stack with its count or an explicit N so the reader is not left guessing; also name what direction an interconnect arrow carries (request vs response) rather than leaving one plain arrow to mean everything.

exemplars.why_chosen: Minimalist variant: plain margin labels 'CNs' and 'MNs', not a boxed band, stand in for the compute/memory-pool split, while colored bold-italic headings (teal Pipeline Execution, red Cache Management) flag the paper's two named mechanisms.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When space is tight, replace the usual boxed interconnect band with a single margin label per tier (CNs / MNs) and rely on it alone to mark the boundary; reuse a bold-italic color per named technique (teal, red) across figures so a reader recognizes the same mechanism later without re-reading a legend.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated symmetric-heterogeneous variant: private caches under two differently-colored protocol domains (pink Intel, purple Arm) read bottom-up through numbered request/response arrows into a shared dashed 'CXL Bridges' band and a shared Global Directory on top.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Give two heterogeneous host domains their own protocol color (pink, purple) that stays constant from their private caches up to the shared bridge, draw the bridge as one dashed band straddling both domains rather than a separate box, and number every request/response arrow even though this traversal runs bottom-up.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated: a green RTOSUnit device plugs into several points of a yellow RISC-V host processor (pipeline, duplicated register file, CSRs, memory arbiter), with lettered interface arrows (a)-(g) keyed to the text instead of a legend.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Color the device you are contributing green and the host structures it modifies yellow so the split is legible at a glance, then key each of its many wires into the host (pipeline, register file, CSRs, memory arbiter) with a letter cross-referenced in prose rather than crowding the figure with a legend.

exemplars.why_chosen: Client-cloud host-device variant: only the two novel modules, blue Game Frame Interceptor and green Remote VSync Coordinator labels, are colored against an otherwise plain black-and-white baseline pipeline (Input Injection, Game Rendering, Frame Encoding).
exemplars.what_to_learn: Leave the reused baseline pipeline plain black-and-white and color only the boxes and labels you are contributing (blue, green here); but unlike this figure, still add a small legend for those colors and draw an explicit arrow for a component like the Remote VSync Coordinator instead of implying its connections by position.

exemplars.why_chosen: Dense 14-component figure whose red-numbered 1-8 sequence overlays a Borrower/Lender pair sharing a coherent memory space, with a top four-color legend (control, command, data, metadata) the reader must cross-reference against numbers placed far below it.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Number the resource-sharing protocol steps in one bold color directly on the repeated peer boxes (Borrower/Lender) so the sequence reads without a key; but place the flow-type legend near those numbers, not at the opposite end of the figure, since this one forces a long eye trip between the two.

exemplars.why_chosen: Double-column, dense figure mirrors the identical learned-index tree on both sides of a dashed NIC-Host PCIe divider, using matched cyan/orange region colors and green-highlighted 'new' nodes to show structural updates crossing the boundary.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Mirror the exact same data structure on both sides of the host/device boundary using two background tints (cyan device, orange host), reuse identical node names on both copies but recolor the ones a structural update just changed, and route curved cross-boundary arrows to carry the sync messages by name (patch, stitch).

exemplars.why_chosen: Medium-confidence, top-down split: a large Local Node (DRAM cache sections, application processes, local Mira Runtime) sits above a small Far-Memory Node running the same-named Mira Runtime (remote), joined by one plain labeled network/interconnect arrow.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Reuse the exact same component name on both sides (Mira Runtime local vs remote) so the reader sees mirrored halves of one system, and let the two sides be unequal in size when one genuinely does more work; keep small repeated cache-section icons visually distinct, unlike here.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated three-zone host-device figure: tan software stack sits above blue gem5 host (CPU/cache/memory simulators) which reaches a pink Accelerator Simulator zone through a dedicated Interconnect Simulator box, with MMIO and DMA arrows individually labeled.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Give the interconnect itself a named box (Interconnect Simulator) between the two color-coded zones instead of a bare arrow, and label the crossing arrows with the actual interface name (MMIO Read/Write, DMA); but unlike here, draw an arrow, not just vertical adjacency, when one box is said to run inside another.

exemplars.why_chosen: Densest host-device figure here (900+ shapes, double column, star-rated): a CPU issues commands over a Shared Buffer to a color-coded 4x4 heterogeneous CGRA tile mesh (red BrT, gold CoT, gray BaT tiles).
exemplars.what_to_learn: Color each tile type in a heterogeneous accelerator mesh by function (red, gold, gray) so the reader sees the mix at a glance, and use dashed insets to zoom into one tile's internal datapath; cap the insets at one or two, since three competing zooms in this figure fight the main diagram for attention.

exemplars.why_chosen: One of the corpus's rare bottom-up host-device figures: a packet climbs from the tan RMT Pipeline through the on-NIC scheduler and load balancer, crosses PCIe, and lands in repeated Core 1...N schedulers above.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Bottom-up is almost never used in this corpus, but it works here because the physical packet path genuinely rises from NIC to host; if your data truly flows upward, orient the figure that way rather than forcing top-down, and repeat the identical per-core sub-structure (Core 1...N) to show scale-out feeding a shared Core Allocator.

exemplars.why_chosen: Medium-confidence but star-rated: five FPGA-resident modules (M1-M5) sit inside one dashed FPGA boundary between RNIC and Host, with an inside legend naming three arrow classes and three numbered circles marking the asynchronous analysis path.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Number every module consistently (M1-M5) so prose and figure cross-reference cleanly, dash exactly the one path the text calls asynchronous while keeping the main forwarding path's arrows solid, and put the two-or-three-color arrow legend inside the boundary box it explains rather than off to the side.

exemplars.why_chosen: Sparse, icon-only figure (9 components, no fill colors): a thin dashed Client box sits opposite a heavier Edge box holding all three intelligence modules, split by a plain dashed-vs-solid legend for control versus content data.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Make the size imbalance do the argument for you: draw the thin client as a small box with only two items while every piece of intelligence piles into the edge/host box, and use icon line art with a single dashed-vs-solid legend instead of color when the point is thin-vs-capable, not many flow types.

exemplars.why_chosen: Deployment-style figure with photographic server and device icons instead of abstract boxes: only the inserted Tooth module is outlined red inside a plain codec pipeline, and three colored lines fan out to three player devices.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When the paper's contribution is one small module inserted into an existing pipeline, outline just that box in red and leave its neighbors plain rather than recoloring the whole chain; realistic device photos can stand in for the host and client, but keep enough labels that arrow direction is not left to guesswork.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated: sender and receiver CIPU diagrams mirror each other with their two offload sub-boxes swapped in order, keying nine circled steps to a middle panel that also draws the packet as colored header segments.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Mirror sender and receiver by swapping the internal order of their shared sub-boxes (Bifrost/AVS becomes AVS/Bifrost) so the drawing itself shows the protocol is symmetric, and key numbered steps to named optimizations plus a packet-format strip in one shared middle panel, accepting the reader must glance away from both diagrams to read it.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three containment levels drawn top-to-bottom (Sorting Engine -> Sorting Core -> MSU+) with the focal unit highlighted in blue.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw each level once, connect levels with dashed leaders, and reserve the accent fill for the innermost novel unit.

exemplars.why_chosen: GPU hardware containment (HBM/L2 -> GPC -> TPC -> SM) with a magnified SM panel to the right; 11 components, 0 flows.
exemplars.what_to_learn: A containment figure needs no arrows at all; repeat the innermost box in a grid to convey count, and magnify one instance for its contents. Note: the print.png carries the paper title line from PDF extraction; preview.png is clean.

exemplars.why_chosen: Deepest clean nesting in the corpus (nesting_depth 4): global memory over computing units over buffers over per-warp regions.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Four levels only stay readable if each level changes exactly one visual property (fill tint, border dash, padding) and text shrinks by at most one step per level.

exemplars.why_chosen: Four stacked drill-down panels (a)-(d) taking the reader from host address space to a single processing engine, tallest aspect here (0.51).
exemplars.what_to_learn: When four levels will not nest visually, stack them as lettered panels down the column and let each panel's caption name its level; add a control-vs-data legend at the level where signals first matter.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar at depth 3: three separate dashed contribution boxes, Coverage Optimizer, Tracing Controller, Memory Allocator, each nest their own two sub-modules inside an outer cluster-to-node container, across 16 components.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Nest each contribution two levels deep inside its own dashed accent box carrying its section number, rather than flattening everything to one depth; keep the same dashed-border-plus-number treatment at every nesting point so a reader recognizes a paper's own module regardless of depth.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star, high-confidence nested-stack exemplar at depth 3: a dashed Solver box contains two title-bar stages, and the inner Parallelism Planner itself contains a further Sequence Bucketing and Parallelism Solving pair, in just 7 components.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Make the outermost container a dashed logical grouping rather than a drawn system boundary, and change only the fill tint between nesting levels, dark-blue title bar to light-blue body, instead of also changing border style, keeping three levels of depth visually calm.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar of the mirrored-replica variant: two identical Worker Machine boxes each contain a CPU region nesting one Feature Cache Engine and GPU regions each nesting one Worker box, to depth 3.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Repeat the identical three-level containment, machine over CPU-or-GPU over its inner engine or worker, in two side-by-side mirrored boxes rather than describing the replication in text, and keep one consistent fill per role across both copies so the eye reads them as the same structure twice.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar with only 6 components: two dashed Worker Node boxes each contain a Scheduler, Executors and a Shared Memory Object Store stacked inside, reached by crossing arrows from two redundant Coordinators above.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Keep a replicated container's internal stack, scheduler over executors over object store, identical in both copies, and reserve one flat colour per role so containment reads correctly without a legend; let the outer dashed border, not colour, be the property that marks one node.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar at depth 3: a dashed Granule box wraps a sandbox box around the application code, while below it a dashed Granny core box nests three named state structures beneath three colour-coded backends.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Use a dashed wrapper box to show an isolation boundary around the code it contains, and let a second dashed box one tier down hold the shared internal state that every parallel sibling box above it depends on, keeping padding consistent at both nesting points.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar spanning a host-device split: the CN side nests its API box inside a runtime box, while the MN side nests a ring buffer and an MWTable, tied together by 5 numbered steps.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Nest a paper's own small contribution box one level inside its host's generic runtime box rather than drawing it as a sibling, and represent an internal data structure like a free list literally as a ring with Head and Tail pointers instead of a plain rectangle.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar at depth 3: a dashed Cilantro Scheduler box nests an Online Learners box that itself nests two Performance Model boxes, alongside a Policy box nesting one highlighted objective, in 11 components.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Nest per-item boxes, one Performance Model per job, inside the shared learner container that produced them, and pick out the single configurable piece with its own inner accent-filled box one level deeper than its parent.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar also cited as the layered template's own gutter exemplar: the LLM Service nests a Manager box that nests four analysis sub-modules, and the LLM Engine nests two modules behind a stacked-instance icon.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Put the tier name in a left gutter even while nesting sub-boxes inside it, and mark a box that stands for many running copies with a stacked-rectangle offset icon behind it rather than drawing every instance, keeping that as the one extra property at that nesting level.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar where a dashed host-side Application Buffers box nests a GPU HBM box that nests its MR descriptor, mirrored by the NIC's own nested Flow Table to MS List to MR Table chain.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Carry one indirection chain, table entry to resource, as boxes nested or linked one inside the next rather than a flat row, and put a boxed legend decoding dashed-versus-solid line meaning directly in the frame when both a management path and a data path are drawn.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar reaching real depth inside one of two dashed panels: LLM Replicas nests a stacked GPU icon nesting Cross-adapter Batching, nesting a Base Model box, nesting two Adapter boxes, four levels deep.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When one side of a two-panel figure is actually a deep hierarchy, let it nest, GPU pool over batching over base model over per-request adapters, while the other panel stays shallow; use one accent colour only for the cross-cutting controller that ties both panels together.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar in monochrome grayscale where the Worker Node box nests a Coroutine Runtime box that itself nests the Batch Oriented Inference Engine and Scheduler side by side, to depth 3, across 15 components.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When colour is not available to mark nesting, use shading depth alone, each level of containment one shade darker or lighter than its parent, and keep the innermost pair of boxes the same size so the reader reads them as siblings at the same depth.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar where the gray Oobleck box nests an Execution Engine box nesting a Pipeline Instantiator and Batch Distributor pair, while the Node Cluster nests repeated Agent groups, one picked out in red dashed.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Nest a sub-engine's own two named components one level inside it rather than listing them beside it, and mark the one instance under discussion, a failing node, by swapping only its border to a red dashed line while every other repeated group keeps a plain solid border.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar where the Planner box nests its own Failure Normalization and Adaptive Schedule Generation steps, and each Executor box in the Training Cluster row nests a small parallelism icon grid, to depth 3.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Give every repeated leaf box, here each Executor, the same small inner icon grid so per-worker internal state reads identically across the row, and reserve the one exception, a red dashed outline on the failed Executor, for exactly the box that differs.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar: the Offline box nests a Profiler and Solver box nesting two hot/cold neuron icon grids, and the Online box nests CPU and GPU Executor boxes each nesting their own dot-grid activation icon.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Carry the same small coloured-dot icon grid, hot versus cold neurons, from the outer profiling box down into each inner executor box so the reader traces one visual motif through every nesting level, and put the icon legend once at the top rather than per level.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar with only 11 components: the Object Storage Service box nests a Proxy Layer box nesting a horizontally repeated Proxy 1 through Proxy n row, three levels of containment for one stateless pool.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Wrap a replicated pool in its own labelled sub-box one level inside the service that owns it, rather than drawing the instances loose in the parent box, so containment alone tells the reader the pool is one interchangeable unit, not several separate services.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star, high-confidence nested-stack exemplar: the dashed Pod-Wide Allocator box nests a Logical SSD Pool and a Logical NIC Pool, each nesting Free, Allocated and Failed sub-boxes, in just 7 components and depth 3.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Split a shared allocator into side-by-side same-shape sub-pools, each nesting the identical three-state vocabulary, free, allocated, failed, so the two resource types stay visually parallel, and reserve one bold colour for the control-path arrows leaving the whole nested block.

exemplars.why_chosen: Medium-confidence nested-stack exemplar reading bottom-up: an outer Transformer box nests the Mixture-of-Experts feed-forward block, which itself nests a Router and its expert FFN boxes, three levels deep, with a stacked background implying repetition.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Nest a sparse sub-block, router plus experts, one level inside the standard block it replaces so the substitution is visible as containment, and show which inner sibling was actually chosen with a bold solid arrow while untaken siblings keep only a dashed candidate arrow.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar where the Coordinator box nests a Profiler, a Placement Planner and a Scheduler stacked inside it, while a separate Compute Node panel nests three alternating Queue and Layer boxes, across 18 components.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack a coordinator's internal stages inside its own labelled box in top-to-bottom order even when the rest of the figure runs left to right, and keep a node's repeated queue-then-layer pairs the same size and colour so the pattern itself shows the pipeline running inside one node.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star, high-confidence nested-stack exemplar: each Compute Node and Memory Node box nests a NIC box that itself nests a three-level protocol stack, MAC and PHY, mirrored on both sides of a V.S. comparison.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw a protocol stack as boxes literally inside the NIC box that owns it, one level per layer, and repeat the identical nest on both compute and memory nodes so a labelled dashed bracket can span just the layers that are the paper's actual focus.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star, high-confidence nested-stack exemplar combining containment with replication: three identical vSSD columns each nest an RL Agent box nesting a Monitor and Model, funnelling into a shared Admission Control box nesting a dashed manager.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Repeat the identical three-level column, agent over monitor-and-model, exactly N times for N replicated learners, and mark a box that is a logical tracking structure rather than a physical component with a dashed border, one level inside the shared infrastructure box it belongs to.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star, high-confidence nested-stack exemplar: each Sender and Receiver dashed box nests a Processor Core box that nests Program Code and a Local Apic, seven numbered steps threading through all three nesting levels on both sides.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Mirror the identical three-level containment, host box over processor core over program code and local APIC, on both communicating parties, and number the steps once across the whole nested structure so the sequence reads correctly despite duplicate box labels on each side.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar on its left half: an outer frame nests Generator, Leakage Model and Executor regions that each nest a Test Case or trace box, four levels deep, at 14 components and 10 flows.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Nest a shared Test Case object one level inside the Generator region that produced it so both consumers can be drawn pulling from the same box; the record's weakness warns that leaving two halves adjacent without a connecting arrow can hide how they relate, so add one even when space is tight.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar reaching four levels: Server Machine nests Storage, which nests the SSD Controller and NAND Flash Memory, which themselves nest Internal DRAM plus three named units and a grid of Flash Chips.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Let a physical enclosure nest its real sub-components exactly as they are physically contained, machine over storage over controller over unit, and reserve a distinct accent colour for the one innermost box, encrypted data, that is the paper's actual security claim.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence nested-stack exemplar across a five-zone swimlane: the DChannel client box nests a Packet steerer and a Reordering buffer, and the mirrored DChannel proxy box nests the identical pair, tied by two colour-coded channel arrows.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Nest the same two named sub-modules inside both a client and its mirrored server box so the symmetry is legible from shape alone, then colour-code the parallel channel arrows between them; the weakness here notes those channel colours need a legend, so add one even for two lines.

exemplars.why_chosen: (a) baseline cluster / (b) proposed cluster with identical bottom anchor box (Shared LLC) so the delta is structural.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Keep one component identical and in the same place in both panels; it becomes the fixed point the reader measures the change against.

exemplars.why_chosen: Explicitly cited in the reference as the matrix-filed baseline-vs-ours exemplar: two small prior topologies stacked left, the larger 3-island Octopus design right, no arrows needed to make the contrast.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack the baseline variants smaller on one side and draw the proposed design larger on the other; use two named link colors (brown for intra-island, navy for inter-island) labelled directly on the drawing instead of a separate legend.

exemplars.why_chosen: Textbook two-panel pair: identical Sender/RNIC/receiver skeleton in both halves, a red X on the failing 384B write in (a) versus the working multi-packet buffer in (b); explicitly listed as a two-panel-filed exemplar.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Keep sender icons, RNIC box, and the receive-buffer/CQ layout in the same position in both panels; mark the single failure point with a red X in the baseline panel, and let the working buffer geometry in the ours panel be the only visual difference.

exemplars.why_chosen: Uses the literal V.S. rule for wide halves: a compact one-line baseline stacked over a wider two-node Ethernet Fabric design, with the paper's contribution named in orange text and bracketed rather than boxed.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When one half is much simpler than the other, stack them top-to-bottom with a horizontal V.S. rule instead of forcing equal-width side-by-side panels, and name the paper's scope with a coloured label plus dashed bracket rather than a boxed outline.

exemplars.why_chosen: Panel (a) sets up the shared vSSD/channel vocabulary, then panel (b) applies the actual contrast: labelled brackets and yellow fill separate hardware-isolated vSSDs (dedicated channels) from software-isolated ones (shared channels).
exemplars.what_to_learn: When only one of two panels carries the actual contrast, use labelled brackets plus a single highlight colour on the winning option inside that panel; but add a legend for the highlight color, since dropping it (as this figure does) leaves the meaning of the yellow fill unstated.

exemplars.why_chosen: Two states of one hotness-tracking bitmap sit side by side, named by claim ('Retain Hotness' vs 'Cooling Down!') in red and blue rather than lettered panels, showing the before/after rule without a formal (a)/(b) frame.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Name the two halves of a before/after pair with a short claim phrase in colour ('Retain Hotness' / 'Cooling Down!') instead of neutral (a)/(b) letters when the labels themselves carry the mechanism's meaning; but note the weakness here: near-identical bitmap grids in both states can be told apart only by arrow colour.

exemplars.why_chosen: Explicitly cross-referenced in the reference guide as a two-panel-filed baseline-vs-ours exemplar: identical Client/App/Kernel/NIC skeleton in both halves, with an in-figure legend and the M/U circles along each trace counting 12 steps versus 4.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Keep the client/app/kernel/NIC stack identical and in the same position in both panels, then let small repeated icons (the M/U marshal circles) along a bottom trace let the reader literally count the efficiency win; note the weakness that placing the legend far above the trace it explains hurts lookup.

exemplars.why_chosen: A monochrome circuit-schematic pair where the same left-to-right signal chain (oscillator, PA, antenna) appears in both panels, and the entire argument is made by (b) visibly containing fewer blocks than (a).
exemplars.what_to_learn: When the contribution is component removal rather than a single marked difference, just draw the simplified signal chain with visibly fewer blocks in the same left-to-right order as the baseline; add the power numbers on the schematic itself, since this figure leaves the savings claim only in the caption.

exemplars.why_chosen: Mirrors the loop/schedule/hardware skeleton in both panels; red fill marks only the CPU-bound Loop box in (a), the one thing (b) fixes by folding it into uniform uTasks on the L0/L1/L2 grid.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Repeat the loop-plus-kernels skeleton in both panels, but colour only the anchor box that changes (the separate CPU Loop) so the eye finds the fix immediately; add a small legend mapping the multi-level L0/L1/L2 hardware boxes back to the simple CPU/accelerator split in (a), a step this figure skips.

exemplars.why_chosen: Stacked (a) naive PCIe-update / (b) packet-driven ZooRoute panels share the same Programmable ASIC anchor box and hash table, with a right-side legend for the gold delivered-by-packet line and only (b) carrying circled steps.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack a simple baseline over the richer mechanism, keeping the outer ASIC boundary identical in both; but number both panels' steps, not just one, since numbering only the proposed half (as here) makes the comparison feel lopsided, and crop tightly so no neighbouring figure bleeds in.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from baseline-vs-ours by the note-writer: single-frame numbered loop (six steps cycling Server Health Monitor to Diagnostics to Hyrax Inventory to VM Scheduler and back) with an online/offline split, not two contrasted panels; this is a control-loop figure, not baseline-vs-ours.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Use a gold/red border legend to separate modified-existing components from newly built ones, and number a closed loop 1-6 with the online portion tinted apart from the offline portion; label every icon on the path, since this figure's unexplained gear icon at step 3 breaks the walkthrough.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from baseline-vs-ours by the note-writer: a single three-stage pipeline (Projection, Sorting, Rasterization) over a shared DRAM bus, where two accent colours mark added units against an uncoloured baseline, pipeline emphasis coding, not a two-halves comparison.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When the contribution is scattered across one pipeline rather than isolated in a second panel, mark each added unit with its own accent colour (here yellow for foveation, blue for load-balancing) against an otherwise uncoloured baseline pipeline, and add an in-figure legend rather than relying on the caption to map colour to purpose.

exemplars.why_chosen: Repeats the identical IF/ID/ROB/FU/MEM/Commit OoO processor block in both panels; a pickaxe icon on the newly embedded contract-check box is the one added element that turns the four-machine baseline into (b)'s two-machine-plus-shadow-logic design.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Reuse the exact processor-block icon across both panels and add a small pictogram (a pickaxe) only on the box that changes, rather than redrawing the whole unit; pair dashed and dotted line styles to distinguish the ISA-level and microarchitecture-level check paths, and add a legend for the icons since none is given here.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from baseline-vs-ours by the note-writer: panel (a) is one overall dataflow of four hardware units, and (b)-(e) each zoom into one unit's datapath, an overview-plus-details composite, not two contrasted designs, so it belongs under composite-figure.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Put the full pipeline as a labelled overview panel at the top, then stack detail zooms of each unit below it using consistent header-bar naming; keep the lettered panels (a)-(e) in reading order so the overview always comes first.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from baseline-vs-ours by the note-writer: three unlike panels, an annotated existing pipeline, a small two-model insight comparison, and a contribution roadmap, form a problem/insight/contributions composite, not one thing drawn twice under two designs.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Chain unlike panels left to right in the order the text argues them: problem, then insight, then contributions, and reuse one colour (here green) across panels to mark everything that is the paper's own idea, from the insight box to the C1-C3 contribution list.

exemplars.why_chosen: Two identical antenna-to-decode pipelines stacked (a) BigStation / (b) Hydra, with the entire contribution shown as a single dashed box grouping ZF/Equal/Demod in (b) to remove one crossbar shuffle.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack the baseline and proposed pipelines with identical per-antenna rows and crossbar shuffles, then mark the one structural change with a single dashed grouping box rather than redrawing the whole stage; label the saved shuffle count explicitly, since this figure leaves the win unquantified.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from baseline-vs-ours by the note-writer: a single left-to-right mechanism diagram (segments to Rate Monitor to Token Update driving Main and Cheque Bucket gauges) draws one system, not two designs side by side; this is control-data, not baseline-vs-ours.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When two mechanisms coexist in one system rather than replacing each other, draw them as parallel sibling boxes (Main Bucket beside Cheque Bucket) fed by one control box with matching gauge icons, and spell the branch condition in words, since this figure's 'if tagged' icon needs the caption.

exemplars.why_chosen: Baseline tree (a) and OCS-mediated topology (b) share one legend and icon set that also covers a bonus (c) panel detailing the OCS's own time-varying state, extending the shared-legend rule past the contrastive pair.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Put a single legend of small coloured icons above all panels so it covers both the contrasted (a)/(b) topologies and a third detail panel; keep the icons visually distinct, since this figure's weakness is several similar small icons that need close reading.

exemplars.why_chosen: Panel (a) uses a literal red X on Sirius's placement versus a green check on SmartSwitch's, and panel (b) contrasts Sirius's multi-hop topology against the SmartSwitch's layered stack, all in one dense 32-component double-column figure.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Use a literal red X for a rejected placement and a green check for the accepted one to make a physical-fit argument at a glance; if a second panel packs two different diagrams together, split them into their own lettered sub-panels rather than one shared label, since merging them (as here) hides the second diagram.

exemplars.why_chosen: Identical L2/L1/L0 privilege-level scaffold repeats in both (a) SPT-on-EPT and (b) EPT-on-EPT panels, with matching circled-number sequences in both halves (not just one) tracing each design's trap-and-resume chain.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Repeat the same privilege-level scaffold (L2/L1/L0) in identical positions in both panels and number the steps in both halves symmetrically, not just one; but cap step markers well below 32 total, since this figure's density makes the two mechanisms hard to compare at a glance.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from baseline-vs-ours by the note-writer: one integrated architecture, not two contrasted panels, where every added component is coloured orange against an all-white existing backdrop, and userspace/kernel form a mirrored pair rather than a baseline/ours split.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Colour every component the paper adds in one consistent accent (orange here) against an all-white backdrop for everything reused unchanged, so novelty reads at a glance across a single dense diagram; add an in-figure legend for the colour and arrow-style key, since this figure relies on caption text the extraction even cut off.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three lettered panels (a)/(b)/(c) chained by dashed leaders, each zooming into a region of the previous one.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Chained zoom: each panel's leader lines start at a marked region of its predecessor, so the reader can follow core -> array -> cell without a caption.

exemplars.why_chosen: A compact block stack on the left with two dashed callouts on the right expanding its two weight matrices.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Insets sit outside the overview and connect back with dashed leader lines from the exact sub-box they expand - never overlap the overview.

exemplars.why_chosen: Background figure that expands left-to-right in three panels, from coarse stages to a full per-layer compute graph.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Progressive expansion left-to-right suits background/context figures; dashed brackets mark the xN repeated block so the expansion stays finite.

exemplars.why_chosen: GPU-wide layout on the left with one SM expanded on the right; accent fill marks the two active decision points across both levels.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Carry the accent colour across the zoom boundary so the same component reads as the same component at both scales.

exemplars.why_chosen: A uniform tile grid with one tile highlighted and exploded into an internal view via a callout wedge.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Highlight the source tile in the grid (different border/fill) before drawing the callout, so the reader knows which of the N tiles was expanded.

exemplars.why_chosen: An exploded-stage exemplar: the numbered main flow (execute_request to Raft Log to Standby Replicas) sends one dashed line to a grey callout box that unpacks steps 2-4, the AST conversion inside the active replica.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Keep the callout's numbering continuous with the main flow (steps 2-4 inside the box pick up right after step 1 outside it), and colour the one active replica differently (purple) from the passive ones (tan) it feeds so the reader can find the source of the zoom at a glance.

exemplars.why_chosen: Also a hub-spoke exemplar elsewhere: the Tower fans dotted control lines to a small Application DAG, and one node's relationship is pulled out into a magnified Captain panel on the right via a curved leader.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When only one instance among many needs explaining, do not draw every instance's internals: pick one, connect it with a curved funnel line to a same-colour detail panel, and let the untouched instances stay as small schematic icons in the background DAG.

exemplars.why_chosen: A star exploded-stage exemplar: a top row of alternating Dense/MoE layer boxes zooms into one MoE Layer's three parallel GPU rows below, with the two AlltoAllv exchanges the paper targets highlighted in red.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Zoom from a layer-level pipeline down into one layer's per-GPU detail below it, and spend your one accent colour (red) only on the operation the paper is actually about, so it reads as the reason for the whole figure rather than one more box.

exemplars.why_chosen: Also a named hub-spoke exemplar: three panels run left to right, Coordinator internals, a colour-typed cluster graph, and one Compute Node's queue/layer chain pulled into a zoomed panel by a dashed connector, legend below.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Chain three different kinds of panel left to right (control logic, then a topology graph, then one zoomed node) rather than forcing one drawing to hold all three, and put a single legend below spanning all of them since node colour and the layer icon both need explaining.

exemplars.why_chosen: Only panel (a) of this 4-panel figure is the relevant instance: a Decoding stack zooms via a dashed line into its four-kernel breakdown, while panels (b)-(d) are unrelated serial/batch/speculative timelines.
exemplars.what_to_learn: A background/definitions figure can carry a small inset inside just one of several panels: zoom the repeated-block stack (Decoder 1...N) into its four internal kernel stages with a single dashed line, and leave the timeline panels beside it in a separate, unconnected visual grammar.

exemplars.why_chosen: A star format-inset exemplar: the six-step client-to-SSD pipeline is grounded by a bottom callout box unpacking the bop_add pseudocode, the new hardware command the whole paper is about.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Put the new instruction's pseudocode in its own framed inset below the architecture rather than inline in a box, connect it to the component that executes it, and keep the six circled step numbers running through both the main flow and the client/server/SSD colour bands.

exemplars.why_chosen: The annotation-rail variant: a five-stage vertical pipeline pairs every stage box with a small red-labelled thumbnail of its output artifact, from a MetaGraph icon down to a per-worker execution-plan timeline.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Give every stage in a vertical pipeline its own small thumbnail icon of the concrete data structure it outputs, aligned in a right-hand rail, so an abstract stage name (Graph Contraction, Wavefront Scheduler) is anchored to a picture rather than left purely verbal.

exemplars.why_chosen: Multiple callouts off one pipeline: four dashed boxes below expand the multisine waveform, channelization, packet-matching and localization sub-steps of a numbered seven-stage top row, ending in a heatmap thumbnail output.
exemplars.what_to_learn: One pipeline can carry several callouts, not just one: hang a dashed detail box below any stage that needs unpacking, keep the circled numbers on the top row as the single reading order, and finish with a thumbnail of the actual output (the localization heatmap) instead of a bare label.

exemplars.why_chosen: Only the top strip is a real inset: thin diagonal lines zoom the packet's Outer header down into its five named fields, the format-inset variant, while the layer-stack and path-mesh below are separate, unconnected panels.
exemplars.what_to_learn: For a format inset, draw thin diagonal lines fanning from the byte-field bar down into a small exploded view naming each field, and highlight only the one field the paper mutates. This exemplar's weakness: it then adds two more diagram idioms with no shared frame or legend.

exemplars.why_chosen: The reference guide's own named example of the zoom pattern: nested DP/PP/Layer boxes are the overview, and a dashed callout expands one pipeline stage into CP/TP sublayers on the right at nesting depth 3.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Mark the exact source of a zoom (one pipeline stage) before expanding it, and keep colour consistent across the boundary (navy/blue on the left reappears inside the right-hand CP/TP detail); budget bigger type than this exemplar did, since its own weakness is text too small for four nested levels.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from overview-with-inset by the note-writer: panel (b) is a different abstraction level (the threading model), not a magnified sub-block of a region in panel (a); no dashed leader connects them, so this is a plain two-panel figure.
exemplars.what_to_learn: The transferable move is two-panel's: stack a software layer directly above the hardware topology it runs on in panel (a), colour-code control/data/network traffic by one shared legend, then reuse the same component names in panel (b)'s separate threading-model view instead of drawing a zoom.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from overview-with-inset by the note-writer: a straight three-stage left-to-right pipeline (its own corpus label) with a user/kernel divider and four colour-coded thread tokens, no magnified callout or dashed zoom anywhere in the figure.
exemplars.what_to_learn: The transferable move is pipeline's: assign each parallel worker (t1-t4) one consistent colour and trace a single one of them (t4, dashed outline) through every stage as the worked example, converging all four at the end into one aggregated operation instead of four separate ones.

exemplars.why_chosen: A textbook zoom callout: HBM/L2 feeding a GPC grid of TPC/SM tiles on the left, with a dashed connector magnifying one SM into its six named internal units on the right.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Colour-code each level of a hardware hierarchy consistently (yellow memory, blue TPC, orange SM, green SM-internals) from the overview straight into the magnified callout, so the reader never loses track of which level of the zoom they are looking at.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from overview-with-inset by the note-writer: a plain three-stage pipeline (its own corpus label) with small decorative rate-over-time sparkline icons beside the inputs, not a magnified sub-block of any drawn component.
exemplars.what_to_learn: The transferable move is pipeline's: give each of several parallel input streams its own tiny characterizing chart, and distinguish repeated content (four differently-shaped models packed in one worker's GPU memory) by both shape and colour, then legend the shapes explicitly, since this exemplar leaves them unexplained.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from overview-with-inset by the note-writer: two side-by-side mechanism panels (its own corpus label control-data) with a small embedded throughput-vs-load chart, not a zoom of a region drawn elsewhere in the same figure.
exemplars.what_to_learn: The transferable move is control-data's: mark both places a request can be dropped in matching red, feed the resulting failure path into one dashed arrow, and let a small embedded performance chart justify the credit-pool adjustment instead of asserting it, but legend the resource icons this exemplar leaves unexplained.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from overview-with-inset by the note-writer: a plain microarchitecture block diagram (its own corpus label pipeline), storage feeding a scheduler, with an inline eligibility-mask icon, but no magnified callout connected by dashed leaders.
exemplars.what_to_learn: The transferable move is pipeline's: draw the concrete bit pattern (1-1-1-0) the mechanism evaluates right next to the step that reads it, but connect it with a line to the specific queue slots it filters and vary the shade of same-coloured boxes, since near-identical orange boxes here need label-reading to tell apart.

exemplars.why_chosen: Two embedded charts, not one drawn callout: a latency heatmap and a Pareto accuracy-vs-latency scatterplot sit beside the router-and-workers architecture, together standing in for the offline Supernetwork Profiler that feeds the scheduler.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When the thing you need to explain is a data-driven decision rather than a drawn component, inset an actual chart (a heatmap, a Pareto curve) next to the architecture instead of forcing it into a box; keep the figure's own colour-coded example queries walking through both the diagram and, implicitly, the chart's axes.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from overview-with-inset by the note-writer: two stacked address-space bars linked by dotted correspondence lines is a memory-mapping diagram, not a zoom; nothing here is drawn small then separately magnified.
exemplars.what_to_learn: For an address-translation figure, stack the two address spaces as parallel bars and connect corresponding regions with dotted diagonal lines plus a labelled fixed-offset arrow, rather than arrows implying data flow; avoid this exemplar's weakness of reusing the label Service VM for two different-scoped boxes.

exemplars.why_chosen: Four numbered stages left-to-right with a single long return arrow along the bottom labelled with what it carries.
exemplars.what_to_learn: The cheapest loop: a straight pipeline plus one labelled return arrow underneath - label it with the artefact ('the updated configuration'), not with 'loop'.

exemplars.why_chosen: Five numbered lifecycle stages arranged around the frame with a separate gray curved arrow closing the loop.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw the cycle as a ring of boxes around the perimeter and give the return path its own distinct colour/weight so it does not read as another stage.

exemplars.why_chosen: Double-column banner (aspect 4.82, nesting 1) where circled numbers 1-7 run forward along the top and back along the bottom.
exemplars.what_to_learn: At extreme width, run the forward path along the top edge and the backward path along the bottom edge of the same strip.

exemplars.why_chosen: System box with an external hardware platform and a red-highlighted optimizer closing the tuning loop back into the system.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Accent-colour only the box that closes the loop; the dashed system boundary then separates 'what we built' from the platform it runs on.

exemplars.why_chosen: A vertical stage-band pipeline (DNN input to Draft to Verify to Momentum Adaptation) with a feedback arrow returning to the Tuning Scheduler, each band tagged with its paper section in a left gutter.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Put section numbers (Sec 3, 4.1...) in a left-margin gutter beside each stage band so the figure doubles as a map to the text, and give the return-to-scheduler arrow its own path along the right edge rather than overlapping the forward flow.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three boxes (tracker / scheduler / execution engine) with numbered arrows 1-4 forming a closed triangle.
exemplars.what_to_learn: A three-box loop needs no ring: place the boxes at triangle corners and number the arrows so the traversal order is unambiguous.

exemplars.why_chosen: Five numbered stages (5.1-5.5) snake across two rows and close with a return arrow to the SM Circuit, and green checks / red crosses on each change make the accept-reject decisions visible inline.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Arrange more than 3-4 loop stages in a serpentine two-row layout instead of forcing a single wide ring, numbering each box (5.1-5.5) in reading order, and mark automatic accept/reject decisions inline with a green check or red cross rather than a separate results table.

exemplars.why_chosen: A left-to-right packet pipeline contains a nested GRU-Memory feedback loop drawn as a dashed curved arrow, with a below-figure legend spelling out STE (Straight-Through Estimator) so the binarization contribution is named, not just colored.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw an internal recurrent feedback loop (GRU to Memory and back) as a curved dashed arrow distinct from the straight solid feed-forward arrows around it, and put a legend below the figure naming any abbreviation (STE) the first time a coloured step appears.

exemplars.why_chosen: A clean two-box loop between Shared Cluster and the Cilantro Scheduler, where both arrows are labelled with what they carry (Per-Job Feedback up, Resource Allocations down) rather than left as bare lines.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Label both halves of a loop with what they carry, not just the fact of a return path: 'Per-Job Feedback' going one way and 'Resource Allocations' the other, so a two-box optimizer-beside-the-spine loop reads correctly without needing numbers.

exemplars.why_chosen: Numbered steps 1-5 trace a full server-to-client-to-server cycle (profile, optimize, deliver schedule, straggler-notify back), with the two tiers colour-coded blue/green and the chosen schedule row picked out in orange.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Number every arrow in the server-client cycle in one continuous sequence, even where it re-enters the server (step 4's straggler notification), and colour the two tiers distinctly (blue server, green client) so the reader always knows which side owns each step.

exemplars.why_chosen: A dispatcher-to-typed-queues-to-typed-engines spine has the Control Plane hanging underneath with double-headed arrows into the dispatcher and both engine columns, the 'optimizer beside the spine' shape rather than a drawn ring.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Split the spine into two colour-coded parallel paths (compute vs communication engines here) and hang the rebalancing controller underneath both, connected by double-headed arrows rather than a single looping line, when the feedback is continuous rebalancing rather than a discrete numbered cycle.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three identical vSSD/RL-agent columns each send an Actions arrow down and receive a labelled Reward arrow back from Admission Control, turning a replicated-grid of agents into a clean multi-instance control loop.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When N identical agents each close their own loop with a shared hub, label both arrow directions distinctly (Actions down, Reward up) on every column rather than drawing one generic pair and implying the rest, and use a dashed border for a logical/tracking structure like the ghost superblock manager that is not a hard component.

exemplars.why_chosen: Two loops close on one spine: generated images feed back into the Image Cache to update future retrieval, while a side Global Monitor watches request/cache-hit rates and steers Model Allocation into the GPU workers.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When a design closes two different loops (a cache-update loop and a side monitor-and-steer loop), keep their arrows visually separated by routing the monitor's loop along one side rather than through the busy centre; thin out labels near the scheduler, since crowding many small labelled arrows there (as here) gets dense to trace.

exemplars.why_chosen: An open pipeline feeds a boxed TreeVQA Controller loop where cluster cards iterate and split, and a zoom callout below expands one cluster's Yes/No decision with a diamond box, the open-pipeline-into-boxed-loop shape.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw the repeating stage as one dashed boxed container (stacked cluster cards) fed by an open input pipeline, and pull the internal iterate/split decision out into a separate zoomed callout below with its own diamond Yes/No box rather than crowding it into the main diagram.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from control-loop by the note-writer: panel (a) is a small CNN+MLP diagram and panel (b) a straight chain (predictor to LDO to controller to action) with no return arrow drawn anywhere; this is two-panel, not control-loop.
exemplars.what_to_learn: A control system is only a control-loop figure if a return path is actually drawn; when the feedback runs through the physical world rather than back into the diagram, either draw a dashed arrow from the output back to the sensing input or file the figure under two-panel or flanked-core instead.

exemplars.why_chosen: Named in the reference as the exemplar for separating one-time setup from a numbered loop: the Offline Partitioner sits in its own dashed box above, while only the Online Planner's four steps are circled 1-4.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Put one-time setup in its own dashed container above the repeating loop and number only the loop's steps (here 1-4), not the setup; give shared dependencies (the training simulator both stages use) a distinct dotted style, but make it heavier than this figure's, whose light dotted 'uses' lines are easy to miss.

exemplars.why_chosen: Two nested loops span camera and backend: a local Approximation-models/Search-algorithm loop ranks orientations by colour, while a second Updated-weights arrow closes a longer loop from the backend's Approximation model trainer back into the camera.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Use small coloured squares as tokens for orientations so rank order and selection show through colour and position, not labelled boxes, and draw both the fast local loop and the slower cross-tier retraining loop as separate labelled arrows; enclose grouped tokens in a light box, since unboxed grouping here is easy to misread.

exemplars.why_chosen: Four numbered stages funnel into one Transactional Oracle Construction box whose own Graph Decycling loop is the only part that repeats, and green check / red cross icons make the final equivalence verdict explicit.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Number the outer pipeline stages once, then nest the one part that actually iterates (graph decycling) inside its own sub-box with a circular refine icon rather than numbering it too; end the pipeline in a check/cross verdict pair so the payoff reads visually. Add a short legend for the icons, since this figure has none.

exemplars.why_chosen: A left-to-right analysis pipeline feeds a dotted-boundary Relational-debugger box whose own Compute-Filter-Refine loop is the only part with a feedback arrow, keeping external tools (Dyninst, RR, PIN) visually outside the system boundary.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw a dotted boundary around your own system's box to separate it from the off-the-shelf tools and inputs/outputs surrounding it, and confine the return arrow to the one internal stage that actually repeats (Refine back to Compute) rather than looping the whole pipeline.

exemplars.why_chosen: A numbered four-step operator-preference-solver control loop sits above a dashed divider from the unnumbered, continuously running WFQ critical path, red arrows marking the two dynamic on-demand interactions against black for static configuration.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack a numbered, slower control/tuning loop above a dashed divider from the unnumbered, fast critical path it configures, and colour arrows by dynamism (red for on-demand interactions, black for static configuration exchange) rather than by which component they touch.

exemplars.why_chosen: A single concrete example (replicas 2 to 3, highlighted red) traces through the reconciliation chain, where small circular reload icons inside the Statefulset and Volume controllers stand in for repeating loops.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Trace one concrete input change (the red-highlighted replica diff) all the way through the system, and use a small self-loop icon inside a controller box to mean 'reconciles repeatedly' instead of a full drawn cycle; but this figure's ellipsis boxes elide most of the actual loop, so show at least one full traversal too.

exemplars.why_chosen: A shaded grey box explicitly labelled 'feedback loop' bounds Explorer's iterative search, drawn in thin bright-blue arrows that visually contrast with the thick gray one-shot arrows carrying code, logs, and the final script.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Bound the repeating search region with a shaded grey box labelled 'feedback loop' in plain words rather than leaving the reader to infer it, and give the iterative arrows a distinct thin bright colour against thick grey one-shot data arrows so the two kinds of flow never get confused.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from control-loop by the note-writer: three side-by-side lifecycle columns (Initialization, Runtime, Management) numbered 1-7 with no return arrow or cycle anywhere; this is a phase-lanes lifecycle figure, not control-loop.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Number steps continuously across adjacent lifecycle columns (1-3 in column one, 4-6 in column two, 7 in column three) instead of restarting the count per column, so the reader can tell setup, runtime, and management apart while still reading one global sequence.

exemplars.why_chosen: Two labelled red Drop points (before CPU processing, at mutex acquisition) merge into one dashed failure arrow, while a double-headed arrow closes a compact feedback loop driven by an inset throughput-vs-load chart.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Embed a small inset chart (throughput vs load) beside the arrow it drives so the feedback signal is visible, not just implied, and give every drop point its own icon; route each to its own arrow rather than merging two distinct drop points into one dashed line, which here can read as a single point.

exemplars.why_chosen: Architecture on top, an aligned Train / Checkpoint / Time lane stack underneath, with a red stall block calling out the cost.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack the timeline directly under the architecture and align columns so a block on the timeline sits under the component that produced it.

exemplars.why_chosen: Two named lanes with a Time arrow and a right-hand legend; overlap between lanes is the entire message.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Two lanes plus one horizontal Time arrow is enough for a pipelining claim; blank cells in the first column show the pipeline fill cost.

exemplars.why_chosen: Offline/online phase boxes on top with the execution pipeline expanded into IO-thread and inference-thread lanes below.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Expand only the phase that has interesting concurrency into lanes; the others stay as plain boxes.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three instance lanes separated by dashed rules, with lane labels on the right and phase brackets underneath.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Lanes (who) run horizontally with labels in one gutter; phases (when) are dashed vertical rules with brackets under the axis - the two never share a device.

exemplars.why_chosen: A minor but real phase device: panel (a) runs one vertical time arrow past stacked Decoder 0/1/2 boxes showing a prompt's blocks processed one at a time, before panel (b) zooms into the per-layer mapping.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When only one stage of a bigger figure is genuinely sequential, don't force the whole thing into lanes: draw one small vertical time arrow beside the sequential boxes (Decoder 0, 1, 2...) and keep the rest of the figure as an ordinary architecture diagram.

exemplars.why_chosen: An unusual phase variant: instead of a horizontal time arrow, five measurement-round labels (t=1us to t=5us) run along the receding depth of a 3D isometric grid of vertex/edge PUs, replacing dashed phase columns with perspective.
exemplars.what_to_learn: A time axis does not have to run left-to-right along the bottom: this figure stacks its five measurement rounds into the depth of a 3D grid instead, which is a legitimate but riskier alternative to labeled vertical phase rules, since perspective compresses the later time steps.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated, the reference doc's own baseline-vs-ours cross-reference for phase-lanes: two column-aligned stacked timelines (Baseline CPU-GEMV, Cocoon-Emb) share iteration boundaries as dotted verticals, with four circled steps and a red Speedup bracket comparing their total lengths.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack the before and after timelines directly on top of each other at the same horizontal scale, mark shared iteration boundaries with dotted verticals so the eye can compare like-for-like, number the optimization steps that shorten the new timeline, and close with one bracket that measures the total speedup.

exemplars.why_chosen: Clean two-panel timeline pair: batch inference's long BCT bracket spans completed sub-batches while shorter SCT brackets mark each one, against interactive inference's TTFT/TPOT brackets over a single token sequence on the same time axis.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Use double-headed brackets to name and measure intervals directly on the time axis (BCT spanning the whole batch, SCT per sub-batch, TTFT/TPOT per token) instead of describing durations in prose, and give each contrasting regime its own panel on the same axis style.

exemplars.why_chosen: The reference doc's own cross-reference for phase-lanes: TrainMover's row and the baseline row sit column-aligned under one shared Training Timeline arrow, so the bottom row's longer gap visually proves the downtime claim without a number.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Put one shared time arrow directly under two stacked system rows drawn to the same horizontal scale, keep matching phases (preparation, switching) column-aligned between them, and let the visual length of the gap, not a caption number, carry the downtime comparison; color-code recurring machine roles (stayer, leaver, joiner) consistently in both rows.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated 4-panel figure where concurrency is the claim: panels (b)-(d) reuse the same Decoding-box drawing but stack one, two, or two-per-request token rows through it to contrast serial, batched, and speculative decoding.
exemplars.what_to_learn: To contrast concurrency strategies, redraw the identical pipeline box two or three times and vary only how many token rows run through it in parallel, letting the row count itself, not new geometry, carry the difference between serial, batched, and speculative execution.

exemplars.why_chosen: A minimal single-lane instance: one repeating Fwd/Bwd timeline runs across the top under one Time arrow, while four numbered SNIP steps hang off it as an asynchronous side process feeding a before/after precision comparison below.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Keep the recurring training loop as one plain lane under a single Time arrow, and let an asynchronous side process (numbered steps in their own color) hang off that lane without sharing its axis; keep the color legend next to the panel it explains, not far below it as this figure does.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from phase-lanes by the note-writer: this is a 4-component control-loop diagram, EnvManager cycling Reset/Action with a self-loop arrow among Reward Worker, LLM Proxy, and Inference Worker; nothing sits along a time axis and there are no lanes.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Read this as a small control-loop or hub figure instead: a self-loop arrow on EnvManager marks its per-instance reset, and the stacked-rectangle icon reused on every box signals many parallel trajectory instances without needing a time axis or lane grid at all.

exemplars.why_chosen: A figure whose right panel hides a real phase device: colored memory squares stack at future time ticks along a labeled Timeline arrow, with a red dashed box marking the window compared against Available Memory.
exemplars.what_to_learn: A future-facing prediction can still use a real time axis: stack small colored usage squares at each future tick (t, t+1, t+2...) under one labeled Timeline arrow, and draw a dashed box around exactly the window your decision compares, here peak projected memory against the available budget.

exemplars.why_chosen: Only the interesting phase gets lanes: the multiplex engine box alone expands into a two-row Gantt of PL and D micro-batches, with dashed sync lines and one Time arrow, inside an otherwise ordinary control-loop figure.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Expand only the one phase with interesting concurrency into a small lanes/Gantt device (rows for PL and D micro-batches, dashed sync lines, one Time arrow) nested inside a single box, rather than converting an entire control-loop figure into a timeline.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from phase-lanes by the note-writer: 'Profiling / Models / Use Cases' are pipeline stage headers, not time phases, and the three parallel branches inside Models are computation lanes converging on a Slowdown score; no time axis appears anywhere.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Read this as a pipeline with parallel converging branches instead: three same-shaped signal-to-slowdown conversions run side by side under a dashed group box, then merge into one combined score; label the arrows themselves next time, since this figure leaves them unlabeled and relying on box-name adjacency.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from phase-lanes by the note-writer: this is a plain top-down layered software stack (interfaces, compiler, runtime, OS/drivers) with zero drawn flows and a small mirrored remote-runtime box; there is no time axis, no lane gutter, nothing resembling a phase.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Treat this as a layered template figure instead: stack the five tiers top-down, each one depending only on the one below, and echo the same fill color on the small remote-runtime box to show it is a copy of the local runtime tier, not a different component.

exemplars.why_chosen: A table-as-lanes variant: each Frame ID is a row and Arrival/Departure time are phase columns in a status table, the oldest incomplete row flagged by an 'Earliest' arrow, paired with a plain device relay diagram.
exemplars.what_to_learn: A phase-lanes device does not need boxes: a literal table works too, with each tracked item as a row (a lane) and each event time as a column (a phase); highlight the one row that matters (here, the earliest still-incomplete frame) instead of adding a separate callout.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated, textbook two-lane Gantt: Rollout Pool and Training Pool are named lanes holding colored phase blocks, idle gaps highlighted red as 'Dependency Bubbles', with a bracket below measuring solo iteration time against a co-scheduled meta-iteration.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Name the lanes in a left gutter (Rollout Pool, Training Pool), keep every block aligned to one shared time grid so idle gaps are visible rather than compressed away, color the red idle blocks as the named defect ('Dependency Bubbles'), and put a measurement bracket under each timeline to state exactly what got shorter.

exemplars.why_chosen: Four-row drill-down: a full 1F1B training-iteration timeline zooms via curved arrows into one transformer block's two-nanobatch overlap schedule, then a single partition's kernel timeline, ending in two Pareto-frontier scatterplots the schedule was chosen from.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Chain three Gantt-style rows at increasing zoom (full pipeline, one block's overlap, one partition's kernels) with dashed separators and curved arrows pointing to the row below, then close with the actual optimization plot the chosen schedule came from; keep one consistent color per category across every row.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated: a coarse lifecycle timeline (Factory to Data Center Operation) highlights one stage, Online SDC Detection, in red and drops a shaded wedge into AEGIS's per-GPU timeline, where circled steps 1-5 flag one suspicious op.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw a coarse lifecycle timeline across the top, pick out the one stage your system owns in a distinct color, and drop a shaded wedge straight down from it into the detailed mechanism diagram, reusing numbered steps to walk sense-then-verify across a per-unit execution timeline inside that mechanism.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated: four Instance Scheduler lanes share one Time axis, blue/green Gantt blocks marked with check or cross insert points, TTFT/TPOT brackets on the bars, and a fourth lane drawn as a dashed ghost for scaling.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Give each parallel scheduler its own named lane under one shared Time axis, mark exact insertion points on the Gantt blocks with tiny check/cross icons instead of prose, measure TTFT/TPOT as brackets directly on the bars, and draw a not-yet-existing lane as a dashed ghost copy to show elastic scale-out.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated round-by-round grid: Round 1-3 columns cross Case 1/Case 2 lanes, each cell showing the same four colored buffer segments so xbar-routed element-wise ops (Case 1) visibly contrast with DMA-buffered reduction ops (Case 2).
exemplars.what_to_learn: When two execution modes need comparing across the same repeating rounds, draw a small Round-by-Round-times-Case grid instead of one long timeline, keep the same colored segments in every cell so the eye tracks what changes, and reuse one arrow color per data item (Block-1/2/3) to trace it across rounds.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated: panels (a) and (b) draw the same GPE0-3 lanes as a Gantt timeline before and after rebalancing, letting shrunken idle gaps argue the fix, before panel (c) shows the scheduler hardware that produces it.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw the identical set of per-lane Gantt bars twice, once unbalanced and once rebalanced, so the reader compares idle-gap width directly instead of reading numbers; but keep labels at a readable size, since this figure's 2-3.5pt text is illegible without zooming.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from phase-lanes by the note-writer: the dashed divider here separates userspace from kernel space, a privilege boundary, not a time axis; there are no phases, no Gantt blocks, only three numbered limitation callouts on an ordinary stack diagram.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Read this as a layered or host-device-style figure instead: stack userspace over kernel space across one dashed boundary the way a PCIe or OS boundary is drawn elsewhere, and overlay numbered red-italic callouts directly on the components a limitation applies to.

exemplars.why_chosen: Two Local Scheduler lanes, each a colored Gantt of micro-request segments (orange prefill, blue decode) on a shared Time axis, sit beneath one Global Scheduler whose circled steps 1-7 close a partition-predict-route-feedback loop.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Split one long request bar into colored sub-segments (prefill orange, decode blue) at the exact token position it was partitioned, lay two such lanes side by side under one Time axis labeled Unified Instances, and close a feedback loop back to the scheduler above with performance metrics rather than leaving the loop implied.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from phase-lanes by the note-writer: this is a before/after comparison (Prior Profiler Arts vs KPerfIR) with an Enables arrow fanning to three example tools, not a timeline; nothing sits on a time axis and no lanes or phases appear.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Read this as a hub-with-fan-out figure instead: put the shared IR at the visual center with 'Semantic' and 'Metrics' callouts, contrast it against the disconnected prior-art pipeline on the left, and fan one Enables arrow out to three dashed example-tool boxes on the right rather than forcing any of it onto a time axis.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three identical worker columns inside one outer boundary with a shared queue, plus an inside legend for link types.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Replicas as columns share a horizontal resource above and below them; the legend then only needs to explain the link colours between columns.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated, high-rank figure the reference doc itself cites as the canonical times-N annotation: 16 identical PIM Ctrl/GDDR6-PIM channels are drawn once, marked '×16', with an inside legend naming inter-device, intra-device, and control flow.
exemplars.what_to_learn: For a very large, fixed replica count, skip the ellipsis and just draw one instance with a bold '×16' label beside it; keep the flow-type legend (inter-device solid black, intra-device solid blue, control dashed orange) inside the frame since it is what makes the single-device diagram legible.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three-tier stack whose bottom tier is one SmartSSD drawn twice with an ellipsis, with novel parts highlighted green.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Replication lives in one tier only; keep the tiers above it singular so the figure does not read as N whole systems.

exemplars.why_chosen: A cautionary case: three concrete Core columns are drawn with no ellipsis at all, violating the template's own 'never three or more concrete copies' rule, even though the stacked Driver/Application/Monitoring bands are cleanly repeated.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Do not draw three or more full concrete replicas side by side as this figure does; collapse to two columns plus an ellipsis (or a Core N column) instead, while keeping its good idea of repeating the same colored Driver/Application/Monitoring bands identically in every column and fanning them back to one Aggregator.

exemplars.why_chosen: A minimal replicated-grid element inside a feedback-loop figure: two Job hexagons plus trailing ellipsis dots sit in the Shared Cluster, each with its own Online Learner performance model feeding one shared Policy above.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When replication is secondary to a feedback loop, keep it light: two named instances (Job 1, Job 2) plus trailing ellipsis dots is enough to imply the pool, while the closed loop between cluster feedback and the policy stays the visual main event.

exemplars.why_chosen: Replication confined to exactly one tier, as the template recommends: only the bottom-most Parrot LLM Engine box carries a stacked-shadow icon for multiple backend instances, while the four layers above it stay singular.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Keep replication confined to exactly one tier of a layered stack, here the bottom engine, by giving only that box a stacked-shadow icon; leave every tier above it as a single box so the figure still reads as one layered system, not N whole systems.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated, the doc's own example of 'offset stacked boxes behind a single one': the Prefill Instance pool and Decoding Instance pool are each one shadow-stacked card, joined only by a labeled KV Cache Transfer arrow.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw a pool of homogeneous instances as one box with an offset shadow stack behind it rather than an ellipsis row, reserve that device for exactly the two pools the paper's contribution separates, and use one labeled transfer arrow (not a generic pipeline arrow) to name the specific handoff between them.

exemplars.why_chosen: A numbered control row over a GPU-server row numbered 0..N with an ellipsis and a dashed annotation pointing at one server.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Number the replica row explicitly (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, ..., N) and use a dashed leader when you need to say something about one specific replica.

exemplars.why_chosen: Cited in the reference doc for both control-data and replicated-grid: repeated identical node boxes fill the Node Cluster, and exactly one is restyled red-dashed to mark the failing instance instead of adding a callout.
exemplars.what_to_learn: To show one failure among many identical peers, restyle just that single node red and dashed rather than adding a separate callout box or arrow; keep circled numbers 1-5 tracing the unrelated job-submission-to-recovery flow so the failure marker and the process flow do not compete.

exemplars.why_chosen: A textbook match for the indexing rule: the coordinator (Scheduler plus KV Cache Manager) sits at left, and Worker 0, Worker 1, ellipsis, Worker N-1 stack at right, each an identical Cache-Engine-plus-Model-Shard card.
