exemplars.what_to_learn: Index replicas from 0 and label the last one N-1 exactly as this figure does (Worker 0, Worker 1, ..., Worker N-1), stack them vertically to one side, and let a single coordinator box on the other side hold every piece of shared state (cache manager, block tables, allocators) so no worker box repeats it.

exemplars.why_chosen: Worker-0 and Worker-N drawn in full with a centred ellipsis, each expanded to nesting depth 4.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Two full replicas with an ellipsis between them beats three partial ones; index them 0 and N so the reader infers the range.

exemplars.why_chosen: Two nested replication devices in one block: FFN 1, FFN 2, ellipsis, FFN N sit inside the MoE layer, while pale-yellow shaded layers stacked behind the whole block imply N repeated Transformer layers.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Nest two replication scales in one figure: an in-line ellipsis row (FFN 1, FFN 2, ..., FFN N) for experts inside a layer, and a background shadow stack for the layer itself repeating N times, then use dashed-vs-bold arrows from the router to show which single expert one example token actually takes.

exemplars.why_chosen: A modest fit: inside a scheduler-centric hub figure, the shared GPU worker pool itself is drawn as small repeated model icons with an ellipsis between two example diffusion models, standing in for an arbitrary-sized pool.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When the replicated pool is only one stop in a bigger routing figure, keep it compact: two small labeled icons plus an ellipsis inside the pool box is enough, leaving the visual weight on the scheduler's queues and the monitor's feedback loop that are the actual point.

exemplars.why_chosen: Stacked VQA-cluster cards (C_i, C_k, ellipsis, C_j) sit inside a dashed TreeVQA Controller box, with one card, C_j, linked by thin connectors to a zoomed panel below showing exactly how that instance decides to split.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw the replicated instances as stacked cards inside one coordinator box, then link exactly one of them by a thin connector to a separate zoomed panel that details its internal decision logic (here a Yes/No split diamond), instead of drawing that logic inside every card.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated: dashed expansion lines fan from Sorting and Rasterization engines to two differently sized unit lists, sixteen Sorting Cores elided as '...' but only four Rasterization Cores enumerated in full since the count is small.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Match the elision to the count: when a repeated unit list is long (sixteen sorting cores here), collapse it with an ellipsis, but when short enough to read at a glance (four rasterization cores), just enumerate every one, using dashed leader lines to expand either list beside the main diagram.

exemplars.why_chosen: A modest fit inside a numbered hardware-block figure: n-1 VM Queue icons plus an ellipsis plus one distinguished LM Queue icon sit inside the LM Controller, echoing the index-and-distinguish-the-last-one replication rule at small scale.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Even inside a single hardware block, use the ellipsis-plus-one-distinguished-instance device for a queue array (ordinary VM queues, ellipsis, one dedicated LM queue) rather than drawing every queue, and number the resulting datapaths with a small color-coded legend the way this figure numbers its four.

exemplars.why_chosen: Canonical fan-in coordinator-over-replicas: 16 identical RX Pipe Manager trapezoids, elided with a vertical ellipsis, converge into one Notification Buffer Manager, while a separate parallel lane keeps the bulk Data FIFO independent of that metadata fan-in.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Fan-in works the same as fan-out: converge 16 elided, identical processing units into one shared manager using trapezoid connectors, and route a second kind of payload (bulk data) through its own separate, differently-shaped lane so the two never look like the same pipeline.

exemplars.why_chosen: The same figure judged for replicated-grid: Instance 1, 2, 3, ellipsis, N sit in one Inference Engine Pool row beneath the Request Buffer and Context Manager, each showing its own row of colored chunk states.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Keep the coordinator (Request Buffer, Context Manager) visually above the replicated pool it drives, index the instances 1, 2, 3, ellipsis, N, and repeat the same per-instance visual device, a row of colored chunk cells, in every box so the reader can read each instance's state directly.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from replicated-grid by the note-writer: this is a three-band privilege-level stack (L2, L1, L0) with one numbered fault-and-fix path stepping down and back up; there is no set of repeated peer nodes and no ellipsis anywhere.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Treat this as a control-loop figure instead: stack the three privilege bands top to bottom, and let one circled 1-5 sequence travel down through the fault handlers and back up, rather than expecting any part of it to show replicated peers.

exemplars.why_chosen: PCIe switches, GPUs, and NICs each run '1 ⋯ 8' with an explicit last index inside this two-panel figure's hardware row, while panel (b) separately elides repeated connections and QPs.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Number the last replica explicitly (1 ⋯ 8) instead of using N when the paper's real hardware has a fixed, known count, and repeat that same ellipsis device at a second scale, connections or queue pairs inside one thread, when the implementation panel needs it too.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star-rated recursive variant: Stage 1 is drawn full-size and detailed, Stage 2 sits beside it at reduced scale repeating the same structure, and a 'Stage 3 ⋯' mark elides every further recursion level.
exemplars.what_to_learn: For a recursive/self-similar mechanism, draw the base stage full size and detailed, then draw the next stage smaller beside it repeating the same shapes, and elide any further recursion with a plain 'Stage N ⋯' label rather than nesting boxes indefinitely; label the one operator (here vector-matrix multiply) once in a foot legend.

exemplars.why_chosen: A thin pipeline where replication is confined to one tier: CPU Node and Memory Node repeat with an ellipsis while the developer layers, network, and accelerator stay singular; every stage carries its own section number.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Confine an ellipsis-based repeat to exactly one tier of an otherwise thin, single-file pipeline (CPU Node ... Memory Node here), and stamp each stage with the paper's own section number instead of a legend; avoid this figure's overly wide aspect ratio, which compresses every stage into a small strip.

exemplars.why_chosen: Two tier columns (our orchestrator | the existing platform) with the critical path highlighted orange straight down the middle.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When your system sits beside an existing platform rather than above it, use two columns and highlight only the path that crosses between them.

exemplars.why_chosen: Only three logical components (clients / brokers / servers) wrapped in two labelled scope outlines that overlap deliberately.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Overlapping labelled scopes let one figure name two protocols over the same three tiers without drawing the tiers twice.

exemplars.why_chosen: Interface -> worker group -> scheduler -> data plane -> launcher, 21 components, 0 weaknesses, aspect 0.9.
exemplars.what_to_learn: A deep tier stack stays readable if each tier is a full-width row of equal height and the flow between rows uses hollow block arrows rather than thin lines.

exemplars.why_chosen: Scheduler / agents / parameter-server tiers with section tags, and two-tone shading separating stable from preemptible tiers.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Tier fill can encode a property of the tier (here: preemptible vs on-demand), not just identity; tag each tier box with its section.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three named planes (Control / Scaling / Serving) labelled in the right gutter with 5 numbered actions crossing them.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Name the tiers as planes in a gutter and let numbered dashed arrows cross plane boundaries - crossing arrows are what makes it a lifecycle, not a stack.

exemplars.why_chosen: Six numbered steps cross three tiers (Client Machine, Server Machine, and the SSD's own internal controller plus NAND flash), with a red 'Encrypted Data' label inside NAND Flash Memory showing matching runs entirely on ciphertext.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Nest a third tier inside the second (the SSD's controller and flash chips inside the Server Machine box) when the real system has a storage device with its own internal architecture, and number every cross-tier hop 1 through 6 so the client-to-flash-and-back round trip reads as one continuous path.

exemplars.why_chosen: A minimal three-hop client-server-kernel chain drawn left to right, with reserved GPU(s) explicitly labelled on the kernel icon and bold double-headed arrows naming the HTTP/WebSocket and ZMQ protocols crossing each machine boundary.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Label the protocol name directly on the arrow crossing each machine boundary (HTTP & WebSockets, ZMQ) instead of a generic line, and use flat, distinct icon colours per tier; a background/motivation tier diagram can stay this sparse since it only needs to set up the problem, not show internals.

exemplars.why_chosen: Five zone columns (User equipment to Base station to Core network to Gateway to Internet) frame a mirrored client/proxy pair, with HBC and LLC drawn as two distinctly coloured dashed paths crossing the same boundaries.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw the network path itself as a series of thin vertical zone columns behind the two mirrored endpoint boxes, and give each of the two parallel channels its own consistent colour end to end; add a small legend naming HBC and LLC, since this figure leaves those abbreviations uncoded.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three full-width horizontal bands (In the container, Physical host, Inter-host) are named in a left gutter as the template prescribes, with colour separating software from hardware from network, though zero arrows leave dependency direction unstated.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Name every tier in a left gutter beside its full-width band and colour-code the bands by kind (software, hardware, network); but always add at least a downward dependency arrow between bands, since this figure's total absence of arrows (a listed weakness) leaves the reader to assume top-down dependency rather than see it.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three full-width tiers (Compute, Block, Persistence) are named in the left margin, each a nested box-in-box (VMs inside the Compute Server, GC/Snapshot Workers inside each Block Proxy), connected top-down by double-headed LSBD arrows.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Nest the repeated internal structure (VMs in the compute tier, GC/Snapshot workers in each block proxy) inside its tier's own box rather than flattening it, and name every tier once in a shared left margin; add one accent colour, since this figure's all-gray palette (a listed weakness) makes component roles hard to tell apart.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from multi-tier by the note-writer: four same-level worker boxes in one row, each marked with a stacked-card icon for many parallel instances; there is no tier stack or network boundary, so this is pipeline/replicated-grid, not multi-tier.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Reuse one small stacked-rectangle icon on every box in a row to say 'this runs as many parallel instances' without redrawing each copy, and give a self-looping component (here EnvManager's Reset) its own tight loop-back arrow rather than routing it across the whole diagram.

exemplars.why_chosen: A numbered three-step path crosses an IPC/LFC trust boundary from the in-process PhOS frontend to a separate PhOS backend, which plugs into any of four labelled checkpoint-image sources (Memory/SSD/RDMA/NVM).
exemplars.what_to_learn: Cross a trust boundary (here IPC/LFC) between an in-process frontend and a separate backend with one numbered arrow, and show a pluggable backend by listing its interchangeable sources (Memory/SSD/RDMA/NVM) in one small box rather than drawing each as a separate tier.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three layers (Cloud, Edge, IoT) are named top-down in the left margin, each split into a dashed management column and a solid programmable column, with a legend mapping three arrow colours to Experimental/Control/Monitoring data paths.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Split every tier into a dashed management column beside a solid programmable-infrastructure column so the same shape-code works at all three layers, and put one legend at the top mapping every line colour and box style used below, so the reader never has to guess a colour's meaning per layer.

exemplars.why_chosen: A literal Internet cloud icon is the network boundary between two dashed, mirrored Client and Server boxes, with one orange Congestion controller and its two red control-signal labels the only asymmetry in a symmetric pipeline.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw the network as a literal cloud icon between two mirrored, dashed-outline client/server boxes with matching internal module counts, and make the one contributed component (the Congestion controller) the only differently-coloured box; add a small legend for that colour, since this figure's green-vs-orange split otherwise goes unexplained.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from multi-tier by the note-writer: a control pipeline (top) is split from a two-cloud WAN topology (bottom) by function, not by stacked machine tiers; this is a control-data split with one bridging arrow, matching its own corpus_template.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When a figure's real split is control-plane pipeline above versus data-plane topology below, bridge them with one clearly labelled vertical arrow rather than several, and reach for stacked tier rows only when boxes represent different machines, not different concerns; name the bridging arrow's endpoint, since this figure leaves it unlabelled.

exemplars.why_chosen: Circled numbers on Server 1 trace a write crossing from local per-thread logs to RDMA-replicated backup logs on Server 2 and Server 3, with a shard-map table (CM) above as the routing tier clients consult.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Number the write path only where it crosses a machine boundary (local append versus RDMA replication to the backup tier), and draw the routing/shard-map table as a small inset table above the tier stack rather than another full box, since compact tabular metadata reads faster there.

exemplars.why_chosen: A three-level stack (Cilantro Scheduler internals, Resource Manager/Kubernetes, and per-job Clients/Job Servers) is connected top-down by red-labelled feedback arrows naming the exact data crossing each level (Res-Perf Data, confidence bounds, allocations).
exemplars.what_to_learn: Label every cross-tier arrow with the exact data it carries (Res-Perf Data, Load Data, confidence bounds, allocations) in red so the feedback loop reads without extra explanation, and nest each tier's internal modules inside a dashed sub-box; add a legend for the box-fill colours, since this figure leaves that coding unexplained.

exemplars.why_chosen: Two components (Controller, GPU Server) sit under one 'Serverless Cluster' label beside a separate 'LLM Inference' detail box, with three named contribution boxes along the bottom pointing dashed arrows up into the parts they optimize.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Label a background sub-system with one umbrella name (here 'Serverless Cluster') so a detail panel can sit beside it without seeming detached, and place each contribution as its own small box below with a dashed arrow pointing up into the exact component it modifies; enlarge label text well past this figure's 4.5-5.5pt, a listed weakness.

exemplars.why_chosen: Four operator-chain variants sharing one backbone, with an inside legend and dashed edges for pruned activations.
exemplars.what_to_learn: For operator graphs, keep the backbone chain identical in every panel and colour only the inserted operators; dashed edges mark edges that do not exist at runtime.

exemplars.why_chosen: A real DAG appears as the input artefact at the top, then reappears as small inline sub-diagrams inside the system's stage boxes.
exemplars.what_to_learn: A DAG can be an inline glyph: draw it small inside the box that consumes it rather than giving it its own panel.

exemplars.why_chosen: Five lettered panels carrying one computation from source code through expression IR to a fused dataflow graph, with consistent colour.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Keep one colour meaning (here schedule vs sparsity) constant across every representation so the reader can track the same tensor across panels.

exemplars.why_chosen: A star exemplar of the graph-editing convention: each of five loop panels draws a branching subgraph, yellow-shaded ambiguous regions, coloured circles for the MaxSAT-solved fix, arranged as a closed 5-panel loop rather than one DAG.
exemplars.what_to_learn: This is really control-loop's shape, not dataflow-dag's, but it still teaches a graph-editing device: shade the ambiguous subgraph region in one flat colour, then redraw the same nodes with green checkmarks or red crosses over each candidate fix so accept/reject reads at a glance.

exemplars.why_chosen: The Application graph is a genuine small DAG (a Gateway node branching into several server nodes that converge again), not a chain, drawn as a compact icon distinct from the hub-spoke control fan-out above it.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw the small application-level DAG as plain blue nodes with simple branching edges, kept visually separate from the dotted control lines that fan out from the Tower above it, so the reader does not confuse the data-flow graph with the control-relationship fan-out.

exemplars.why_chosen: The inline-glyph variant: a tiny Computation Graph icon of two branching tasks sits at the very start of the pipeline, exactly the 20-30pt DAG-as-icon convention the template calls out, feeding into a five-stage annotated planner.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When a DAG is only the trigger for a pipeline rather than the figure's subject, shrink it to a small multi-coloured icon (20-30pt) rather than drawing it at full scale, and let the rest of the figure show what consumes it.

exemplars.why_chosen: The Tile-graph row shows a real merge, two input nodes converging into the first operator, before flowing through alternating orange/blue nodes, nested inside a layered compiler stack down to a memory hierarchy.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Even a mostly-linear operator graph earns dataflow-dag treatment the moment two nodes merge into one, so draw that merge explicitly (two boxes, one arrowhead) rather than smoothing it into a chain, and carry a highlighted path in one colour (red) down through the memory-hierarchy bands it maps onto.

exemplars.why_chosen: A star exemplar: the Graph Optimizer panel stacks three small labelled graphs, each with visible branching nodes, to show three different query-specific dataflow-graph optimizations produced from the same declarative input.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack two or three small example graphs inside the box that produces them to show a family of possible transformations, using small filled and outlined circles for operators; label each of the three so a reader can tell which optimization pass produced which graph, since this exemplar leaves that unlabelled.

exemplars.why_chosen: The SA-DFG mini graph at top (Step, Cast, FWD, BWD nodes with per-node GPU/CPU cost labels) is the dataflow-dag content, sitting above a larger host-device split showing the five techniques it motivates.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Annotate each node of a small operator graph with the cost it would incur on each of two heterogeneous processors, so the graph itself argues for offloading; keep that graph compact and separate from the larger host-device architecture it motivates below it.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from dataflow-dag by the note-writer: a plain five-box left-to-right pipeline; the 'Serverless Graph' is a named artifact passed between boxes but never actually drawn as nodes and edges anywhere in the figure.
exemplars.what_to_learn: The transferable move is pipeline's: run coloured dashed bands along the bottom naming which paper section documents each stage, and group the plugin-style services (S3, SQS, Pub/Sub) as small icons inside one stage rather than drawing each as a separate box.

exemplars.why_chosen: A genuine branching computation graph: coloured grid cells for two modalities and a backbone are linked by red curved data-dependency arrows crossing rows, feeding a tree-search icon and a pipeline-interleave grid.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Colour each node by which of several node types it belongs to (green/orange/blue for the three modality classes here) and let curved red arrows, not orthogonal routing, carry the cross-row data dependencies; pair the graph with a small tree icon standing in for the search procedure that reorders it.

exemplars.why_chosen: The LoD trees are real branching graphs, colour-coded by reuse state per node, with a red cut line marking the frontier, and a separate small subgraph diagram showing the client's local update.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw a hierarchy that gets pruned as a tree with a red cut line across it marking the current frontier, colour each node by its reuse/cache state rather than its type, and put a 3-colour arrow legend at the top since this dense a figure otherwise relies entirely on it to separate three overlapping flows.

exemplars.why_chosen: The tensor operator graph (op1 and op2 merging into op3) and the per-device training DAG sit as small inline glyphs beside the four-step App/Comm Layer stack they illustrate, at high confidence.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Place a small branching operator graph and a per-device schedule diagram beside the pipeline stage that emits them rather than inside the stage box, and keep the layer-group brackets (App Layer, Comm Layer) tight against the boxes they enclose, since this exemplar lets them drift visually apart.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from dataflow-dag by the note-writer: three dashed-bordered layers stacked with zero arrows anywhere; the only nod to a graph is a box labelled Computational Graph, never drawn as nodes and edges.
exemplars.what_to_learn: The transferable move is layered's: highlight only the paper's own novel boxes in one accent colour, here purple on exactly four of twenty components, against plain white boxes, so contribution versus reused building block reads instantly even with no arrows at all.

exemplars.why_chosen: The DFG of operators, two round nodes, A into B, sits directly above the sTask-partition box as an inline glyph, then recurs as coloured A/B tiles through scheduling and hardware mapping.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw the operator graph as small circular nodes beside the stage that consumes it, keep one colour per operator (blue A, orange B) as it moves through partitioning and onto heterogeneous execution units, and close the loop with a labelled Profiling arrow feeding measurements back into an earlier stage.

exemplars.why_chosen: A star exemplar: blue Vertex boxes V1 to VD form the labelled DAG search space, then curved edges in Search Space Relaxation connect them before Discretize turns the graph back into purple Layer boxes.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Carry the same small coloured-square operator code through every stage, layer boxes to superproxy bars to DAG vertex boxes, so identity survives four transformations without a fresh legend each time; add a real legend regardless, since none decodes what the squares mean here.

exemplars.why_chosen: The small diamond-shaped graph inside the purple core is drawn twice, plain then recoloured green/blue/orange, the transformation-arrow variant showing exactly which nodes Module Injection, Kernel Replacement and Overhead Reduction touch.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Show a transformation as the same small DAG twice, before plain and after recoloured, with an arrow between; match each recoloured node's fill to its named optimization label outside the graph, but add explicit callout lines since colour and adjacency alone leave that mapping implicit here.

exemplars.why_chosen: Panel (a) draws a genuine hierarchical DAG, LD/XOR/add nodes grouped by dashed motif outlines, and links it with red leader lines straight to the ALU, router and ALSU that execute it in panel (c).
exemplars.what_to_learn: Group recurring three-node motifs in the dataflow graph with dashed outlines, then draw red leader lines from each motif straight to the physical ALU, router or ALSU tile that executes it, so the graph-to-hardware mapping needs no separate legend.

exemplars.why_chosen: Beside the five-stage MLIR pipeline, a separate inset walks one small DFG (ph1/mu1 inputs merging through add nodes) through Generation, Tuning and cycle-mapped Mapping, the DAG-inside-a-pipeline variant of this template.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Nest a compact three-step DFG-evolution inset, generation, tuning, cycle-mapped scheduling, beside the main pipeline row instead of folding it into the stage boxes; tie the inset to the top bar visually, since here it reads as a detached second figure.

exemplars.why_chosen: Panel (b) traces read-after-write dependencies with curved orange lines from an instruction stream into a small branching DAG of latency-annotated nodes, one of three dense panels at 22 components total.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Build the DAG panel directly from a labelled instruction stream by drawing curved dependency lines from each entry to its node, in a colour distinct from the architecture diagram's plain arrows, and pair it with a schema panel of the tables that track per-node state; keep node labels specific, not generic.

exemplars.why_chosen: The Control plane's LazyDAG is a real branching graph: telemetry triangles and an anomaly feed green expert-diamond nodes (RC1 to RC3) that merge into orange root-cause boxes, at medium confidence.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Colour-code a small live DAG by node role, blue/cyan structure, green computation, orange merged output, light-blue triangles for inputs, and pair it with a small-multiples grid of the same icon style for a library holding many such graphs.

exemplars.why_chosen: The left DFG uses small blue Remote-Pipe circles and an inline Main/Merger/Regular legend to show two pipe-chains, blk1 and blk2, actually merging at a sort -m node, all tied to prose by A1-A6/B1-B4 callouts.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Key a pipe-chain DFG with an inline colour-swatch legend right next to the graph, mark actual merge points with a small circle glyph, and tag every region with letter-number callouts (A1-A6, B1-B4); keep the DFG's pipe-chain style and the downstream box architecture visually consistent, since here they read as two stitched figures.

exemplars.why_chosen: Panel (a) draws the same Conv3x3/Relu/Add subgraph three times, original then after intra- and inter-expression derivation, marking only the newly discovered red eOperator boxes against unchanged tan ones across all three steps.
exemplars.what_to_learn: To show a graph transformation, redraw the exact same operator graph two or three times under labelled derivation arrows and colour only the newly discovered operators red against unchanged tan ones. Qualify reused names like Matmul per panel, since bare repetition across panels can blur which instance is meant.

exemplars.why_chosen: Six panels reuse one green/orange/red op-node vocabulary, Element-wise, Compute-intensive, Reduction, defined once in a legend at the bottom, to show the same neural-network graph being formulated, rescheduled, tuned and finally fused into a Monolithic Kernel.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Carry one small set of node-colour meanings across all six panels, and run a single shared example, SIS1, SIS2, CI Op, through every stage so a reader tracks one case end to end. Repeat the legend near the top too, since it sits only at the bottom here, far from the first panels.

exemplars.why_chosen: Panels (a) and (b) repeat an identical VM/Host-Software/SmartNIC/Disk stack to contrast two data paths, then (c) duplicates that same stack across source and destination hosts linked by one dotted copy arrow, under one shared legend.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Reuse two copies of the same vertical stack side by side to depict a migration protocol (source host, destination host) rather than inventing new geometry, and put one legend to the right covering every line style (solid double-headed, red dashed, black dotted) used across all panels.

exemplars.why_chosen: Panels (b) serial, (c) batched-parallel, and (d) speculative-parallel decoding reuse the same Decoding-block-plus-token-square vocabulary to isolate what changes, while panel (a) above supplies the architecture the tokens flow through.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Keep the comparison panels (here serial vs batched vs speculative decoding) at one shared scale and icon set even when an unlike architecture panel sits above them; but size and align comparison panels consistently, since this figure's four differently sized sub-panels are flagged as visually busy.

exemplars.why_chosen: Panels (b) and (c) repeat an identical four-stage Cross-Attention/Attention/Cross-Attention/Attention stack, swapping only Spatial+Temporal for Full+Full attention, while panel (a) shows the same DiT Block repeated N times around them.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Keep every box in the exact same position across the compared panels and change only the swapped-in stage's label and colour (here Spatial+Temporal versus Full attention); give the two swapped stages more distinct colours than a shared light-blue fill, since this figure's near-identical palette makes the difference easy to miss.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three same-scale baseline architectures (Digital PUM, Analog PUM, Naive Hybrid PUM) reuse one crossbar-array icon throughout so structural differences, an off-chip CPU link versus stacked on-chip controllers, are directly comparable panel to panel.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Reuse the identical crossbar-array icon at the same visual scale across every alternative-design panel so the eye compares structure, not icon style, and letter the panels (a)(b)(c) with short claim titles naming each design; pair the figure with the performance numbers it motivates, since the panels alone (a listed weakness) omit that data.

exemplars.why_chosen: Named in the reference as the three-panels/one-varying-mechanism exemplar: identical SM-roster-to-Tile-to-RS layout stacked as three wide rows, changing only which hardware resource, copy engine, specialized SM, or co-located SM, drives communication.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack comparison panels as full-width rows, not side-by-side columns, when each panel is itself a wide strip, and keep the tile-to-signal-to-RS-unit layout pixel-identical across rows so only the swapped hardware resource (copy engine, specialized SM, co-located SM) catches the eye.

exemplars.why_chosen: Panels (b)-(e) are near-identical small multiples of the same ion-trap grid, boxed in a dashed 2x2 group that zooms into the shuttle steps behind panel (a)'s single collective-swap overview, with orange arrows tracing each step.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When more than four panels are needed for a step-by-step breakdown, group the small-multiple steps into their own dashed 2x2 box rather than spreading all panels across one row, and keep every step's grid icon pixel-identical so only the orange shuttle arrow's position changes between them.

exemplars.why_chosen: A single numbered thread (circled steps 1 through 12) runs continuously across all three panels (Normal execution, Barrier control point, Migration), unlike figures that restart numbering each panel, tying one scenario together end to end.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When three panels show one continuous scenario, number the steps once across all of them instead of restarting per panel, and reuse the same backend colour coding (red MPI, green POSIX) from the architecture figure so panels cross-reference cleanly; budget more room per step than this figure's dense twelve-step layout.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three motivating vignettes (A multi-agent workflows, B multiple fine-tuned models, C personalized agents) reuse one visual grammar, a shared source fanning into separate purple/green boxes, each needlessly reprocessing the same content.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Repeat one simple visual grammar (a shared input fanning into separate coloured boxes) across several real-world vignettes to argue a problem is general, even when each vignette's icons differ; but label what the colours mean on the first panel, since leaving it unstated across all three forces the reader to guess.

exemplars.why_chosen: Named in the reference as the three-lettered-mini-pipelines exemplar: (A) compression, (B) single-chunk prefetch, and (C) scattered prefetch each reuse the identical guest-memory-bar and file icons so the reader compares how each restores memory.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Give each lettered mini-pipeline its own identical anchor icon (the segmented guest-memory bar) so a reader can diff panels purely by which cells fill or how arrows route into it; box the hardware-stage names as real components rather than plain arrow labels, since leaving them as labels, a listed weakness, blurs component from operation.

exemplars.why_chosen: Named in the reference as the NoDG/FuDG/PaDG exemplar: all three strategies reuse the same Scheduler-Instance-LLM-Model vocabulary and green/blue Prefill/Decode legend, and the ours panel (c) comes last with the extra inter-instance scheduling arrow.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Put the paper's own design last with one extra visible element (the dashed inter-instance scheduling arrow) beyond the baseline panels, while keeping the Scheduler-Instance-Model vocabulary and colour legend identical across all panels; place the legend next to the panel where colour matters most, since here it sits far from panel (c).

exemplars.why_chosen: Named in the reference as the bare-metal/VM/SmartNIC-of-increasing-complexity exemplar: panels (b) and (c) reuse the VM0/VM1/QEMU-KVM/NICs skeleton from (a), adding only the SmartNIC internals plus two colour-coded numbered paths in (c).
exemplars.what_to_learn: Grow the panels by increasing complexity while reusing the prior panel's skeleton wholesale (VM boxes, QEMU/KVM, NICs) so only new hardware stands out, and overlay two independently coloured numbered paths (data-plane blue, control-plane red) on the final panel rather than adding a fourth; keep each path shorter than this figure's dense two-by-five overlay.

exemplars.why_chosen: Named in the reference as the three-data-centre-networks exemplar with one legend row: (a) static tree, (b) reconfigurable OCS graph, and (c) the OCS's own time-varying state share one cyan/gray/gold icon set spanning all three panels.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Put one legend row above all three panels rather than repeating it per panel, and let a third panel depart from the first two's topology style to show internal behavior over time, as long as it reuses the same colour vocabulary; keep legend icons visually distinct, since similar small icons here need close reading.

exemplars.why_chosen: Named in the reference as the three-temporal-states-stacked exemplar: online recording, offline buffering, and replay restoration reuse the identical R1/R3-Shim-R2 skeleton, changing only which structure, log or buffer, and which call is highlighted.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack temporal-state panels top to bottom with an identical endpoint-shim-plane skeleton in each, changing only the buffer/log structure and the highlighted system call; number each panel's own steps locally if they are truly separate states, but say so, since this figure's reused 1-6 numbering across panels (a weakness) can look like one global sequence.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from n-panel-comparison by the note-writer: three Pod boxes are simultaneous identical peers in one system, not alternative designs or moments, and the lettered (a)(b)(c) tags label arrow types within one diagram, not separate panels; this is replicated-grid, not n-panel-comparison.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Reserve lettered (a)(b)(c) tags for distinct panels, not for naming different arrow or relationship types inside one diagram, which just needs a legend instead; draw N simultaneous identical peers (here three pods) as a repeated unit feeding one shared control plane below a dashed divider, replicated-grid's job, not a panel-by-panel comparison.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three side-by-side NIC architectures (RNIC, on-path SmartNIC, off-path SmartNIC) reuse the same NIC-cores/PCIe/Host-DRAM skeleton at growing complexity, with circled path numbers kept consistent across all three so the paper can cite them the same way.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Reuse the same numbered path labels (here 1-4) across every panel of a growing-complexity comparison so the numbers become the paper's stable vocabulary for referring back to specific communication paths later, and grow the skeleton by adding new boxes (the SoC) rather than redrawing it.

exemplars.why_chosen: All three panels are three-step (i)-(iii) before/after derivations using the same tensor-cube glyphs and red-eOperator-vs-tan-predefined-operator colour code, letting EinNet's own Matmul+OffsetReduce rewrite in (b) be compared directly against classic im2col in (c).
exemplars.what_to_learn: Give every panel the same internal (i)/(ii)/(iii) numbering and one colour code (red for the paper's new operators, tan for predefined ones) so a novel rewrite and a textbook baseline sit side by side and compare step for step; qualify reused names per panel, since repeated labels (DLT, Matmul) without qualification is a listed weakness.

exemplars.why_chosen: Six panels share one legend on the right: the top row frames the code-versus-hardware connectivity gap with a red 'Gap!' arrow, and the bottom row redraws the identical four-qubit circuit to compare swapping against bridging.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When more than four panels are needed, arrange them as a labelled grid (here 2 rows of 3) with one qubit-colour legend on the side covering every panel, and let a bold callout arrow (the red 'Gap!') point between two panels to name the specific mismatch the rest of the figure resolves.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from n-panel-comparison by the note-writer: three diagram kinds, a tile/tensor layout, a circuit-style instruction-issue diagram, and a buffer-by-iteration timeline grid, explain one design from three angles rather than repeating one drawing under different designs; this is composite-figure, not n-panel-comparison.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When three panels each use a different diagram type (a data-layout grid, a circuit diagram, a scheduling timeline) to explain complementary aspects of one system, file the figure as composite-figure with a dominant panel, not n-panel-comparison, which needs one shared drawing style repeated across the panels.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from n-panel-comparison by the note-writer: three linked stages, covisibility detection feeding tracking feeding mapping, form a pipeline in three different diagram styles where one upstream signal gates two downstream decisions; this is pipeline or composite-figure, not N comparable alternatives.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When one upstream signal feeds two downstream decision paths in sequence, draw it as a linked pipeline with arrows carrying that signal forward, not as side-by-side comparison panels; let each stage keep its natural diagram type (block-matching grid, neural-net flowchart, point-cloud view) since forcing one shared vocabulary here would flatten real differences.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from n-panel-comparison by the note-writer: panel (a) is one systolic-array overview and (b)-(h) are seven different circuit-block zooms, each a distinct block, not repeated copies of one drawing; this is composite-figure or overview-with-inset, not n-panel-comparison.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When lettered sub-panels each show a different, unique circuit block rather than the same block under different conditions, treat the figure as an overview with several distinct insets, not a comparison; keep one consistent colour-phase code (as this figure does) so each inset still maps back to its place in the main dataflow.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from n-panel-comparison by the note-writer: a single pipeline diagram with lettered arrows (a)-(e) indexing prose explanations of signals, not separate comparison panels; there is only one frame here, not multiple copies of a drawing.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Reserve lettered tags for indexing prose explanations of individual signals on one diagram (as this figure correctly does) rather than assuming letters always mean separate panels; box exactly the stages that changed (here the out-of-order I/X/W group) and colour only the new components, leaving the rest uncoloured.

exemplars.why_chosen: Panels (b) and (c) reuse an identical DNN-icon-pool skeleton to contrast preemptible against FIFO multi-DNN scheduling, stacked beside numbered step markers 1-3 in panel (a) that trace the costly weight path each scheduling choice repeats.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack a small pair of identical-skeleton scheduling-strategy panels (preemptible vs FIFO) beside a larger numbered hardware-path diagram so the reader sees both what the cost is and how scheduling choice repeats it; keep the hierarchy labels larger, since this figure's high shape density is a listed weakness.

exemplars.why_chosen: Panels (a) and (b) repeat the identical Server-Switch-Chassis topology with only the highlighted flow pattern (interleaved vs orthogonal) changed, while a smaller inset (c) supplies the generic port architecture referenced by both.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw the same topology twice and change only which flow colours are highlighted to isolate one variable (interleaved vs orthogonal sharing), and attach a smaller generic-component inset for shared internals rather than repeating it inside each main panel; label every flow's endpoints directly, since this figure leaves them to be inferred from the text.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three goal panels separated by dotted lines reuse the same bank/Client/Log icon trio, changing only which actor is tinted red as untrusted, a small-multiples pattern the ranking script flagged low confidence despite the clean fit.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Separate small-multiple goal panels with a plain dotted vertical line rather than a full frame, and keep the same three actor icons (bank, client, database) in every panel, changing only which one is coloured red to mark the untrusted party; label each panel's goal in words, not a letter, when the goal is the title.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three panels re-explain the identical five-layer hierarchy three ways, as a shaded containment stack, a matching software stack, and a colour-coded read/write/reset I/O path, so a reader maps one layer across all three views.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Re-draw the same N-layer hierarchy as three complementary views (a shaded containment stack, a software stack, a coloured data-path diagram) with layers aligned row by row so a reader traces one layer left to right; add a real legend box for the colours instead of inline coloured text, a listed weakness here.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three architecture rows (MCG-X, Google Android Emulator, DroidCloud) are stacked as wide strips sharing one downstream Host pipeline, with red VSync markers and per-hop latency numbers annotated on each row instead of a data table.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack architecture rows as wide strips that converge into one shared downstream pipeline on the right, and annotate per-hop timing numbers directly on the arrows in red rather than a separate table; still add a legend for what red text and dashed VM/Container boundaries mean, since this figure has none despite using both.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three unlike panel kinds sit together, a hash-mapping diagram (a), a rendered 3D voxel illustration (b), and a sad-face/happy-face pros-cons box pair, all sharing the yellow-cell storage-icon vocabulary from the technical panels.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Pair a technical diagram with a small icon-based pros/cons box (a sad face for the limited baseline, a happy face for the improved design) placed right beside it, reusing the same cell-shading vocabulary so the emotional icon reads as a direct verdict on the adjacent architecture rather than a separate aside.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three diagram idioms, a zoomed packet-header byte table, a tenant/overlay/physical layer stack, and an abstract path mesh, share one gold/orange/green colour thread (the mutable outer source port) but no dividing frame or legend groups them.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Even when three unlike diagram idioms (byte table, layer stack, path mesh) share one colour thread across a mechanism, still give each panel its own frame or gutter and one shared legend, since this figure's absence of both, a listed weakness, makes the three parts read as unrelated at first glance.

exemplars.why_chosen: Panel (a)'s coarse per-decoder timeline sits beside panel (b)'s detailed per-layer device map, sharing one blue-single-device/green-multi-device legend so the reader sees which decoder runs when and which of its layers pay the broadcast/gather cost.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Pair a coarse timeline/mapping overview with one detailed per-layer zoom, and carry a single two-colour legend (single-device vs multi-device placement) across both panels so the coarse view and the fine view never need separate keys.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three panels zoom successively from the whole CIM core (a) into one CIM array (b) into its memory-circuit detail (c), each joined by dashed leaders exactly as the overview-with-inset-inside-composite rule prescribes.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Chain dashed zoom leaders panel to panel (core to array to cell) rather than drawing every level from scratch, and keep the same green-buffer/gray-blue-control/light-blue-array colour roles at every zoom level so a reader always knows which block is which even after three levels of nesting.

exemplars.why_chosen: Token-sequence diagrams for vanilla (a) and speculative (b) decoding sit beside a roofline throughput plot (c), a genuine mix of diagram and chart kinds tied together by one shared token-colour legend.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Put a measurement plot (here a roofline chart) beside the mechanism diagrams it justifies, and reuse the diagrams' own colour legend (prompt/drafted/accepted/rejected tokens) as the one legend for the whole figure so the plot and the diagrams read as one argument, not two attachments.

exemplars.why_chosen: An abstract agent-loop diagram (a), a concrete annotated text trace (b), and a stacked latency bar chart (c) are three genuinely unlike kinds under one figure, exactly the box-plus-workflow-plus-plot mix this template is built for.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Let the dominant architecture panel set the organizing idea (the dashed Region A/B boundary) that the unlike trace and chart panels beside it echo, and give each differently-styled panel a light divider or frame, since running three visual languages together with none, as here, blurs where one panel ends and the next begins.

exemplars.why_chosen: Named in the reference as the architecture-beside-two-result-plots exemplar: the dominant microservice graph sits beside a raw P99 scatter and its smoothed average, using two unrelated colour codes, role at left, method identity at right.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Give the dominant architecture panel over half the figure's area and let the two result plots (raw and smoothed) sit as clearly smaller subordinate panels; keep separate colour codes for structural role versus method identity fully apart, since sharing one figure without a divider (a listed weakness) risks a reader reading the wrong key.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from composite-figure by the note-writer: three block diagrams (flow control, retransmission, ICRC pipeline) are fully independent modules with no shared component, dominant panel, or dataflow between them; the rule that unrelated panels are two figures, not one, applies directly.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When three block diagrams genuinely share no component or dataflow, do not force them into one composite just to save space; either draw a connecting line to the larger system they belong to, or split them into separate figures, since grouping unrelated modules under one caption reads as three mini-diagrams, not one architecture.

exemplars.why_chosen: Named in the reference as the namespace-tree/request-flow/sharded-tables exemplar: the tree and RPC diagram sit above four database tables, with matching green object-metadata highlights and red annotation callouts linking letters like C/D/E/G across all three parts.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Let a small worked example's node/id labels (C, D, E, G) recur identically across the tree, the RPC-flow diagram, and the resulting database rows so a reader can trace one concrete write through every representation; but keep the cross-references few, since needing to match letters across three dense sub-panels, a listed weakness, adds real effort.

exemplars.why_chosen: An architecture pipeline, a symbol-definition notation key, and a colour-coded worked example sit side by side as three unlike kinds with no visible borders between them, a violation of the clear-gutter rule the template requires.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Leave an explicit 8-12pt gutter (or a thin frame) between an architecture panel, a notation key, and a worked example even when they logically belong together, since merging three conceptually different sub-panels with no visible border, a listed weakness here, makes the figure read as one crowded panel instead of three legible ones.

exemplars.why_chosen: Panel (a)'s software row/column access diagram and panel (b)'s DRAM-bank-plus-PIM hardware grid are two unlike kinds, software beside a hardware data structure, joined only by the shared insight that ADE/IDE mirrors OLTP/OLAP access.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Use matching colour underlines (green for the specific row or column each side accesses) across a software panel and a hardware grid panel to make an analogy visible without arrows connecting them; add at least one numbered pointer between the panels, since this purely motivational figure otherwise relies on the reader inferring the connection.

exemplars.why_chosen: Before (a) and after (b) Gantt-style GPE timelines share an identical per-lane skeleton to show reduced idle gray time, while panel (c) mixes in the scheduler/workload-table/alpha-buffer hardware that implements the rebalancing.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Pair an identical-skeleton before/after timeline (same GPE lanes, same block width) with a separate hardware block-diagram panel that implements the fix, mixing a timeline kind with an architecture kind under one figure; keep font size well above this figure's illegible 2-3.5pt, a listed weakness.

exemplars.why_chosen: A 4x4 chip-mesh topology overview (a) is joined by a dashed leader to a zoomed single-chip block diagram (b), the overview-with-inset-inside-composite pattern, with the zoom revealing the Control Unit/HN Array/VEX/Buffer stack over shared HBM.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Zoom a dashed leader from one node in a repeated mesh topology into a single expanded block diagram rather than drawing every node's internals, and spell out abbreviated module names in full (this figure's 'Inter. Engine' is ambiguous without the caption, a listed weakness) so the inset stands on its own.

exemplars.why_chosen: A stepwise zoom runs from the 16-core Sorting Engine list into one Core's layout, then into the MSU+'s dual-buffer filter-and-mux detail, joined by dashed lines, with the final, most-novel block highlighted in light blue.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Chain dashed zoom connectors through two levels (engine to core to sub-unit) and reserve one accent colour (light blue) for only the deepest, most novel block so the eye knows exactly which of several nested boxes is the actual contribution; label every symbol explicitly, since this figure's unlabelled '>' comparator relies on visual convention alone.

exemplars.why_chosen: Panel (a)'s labeled architecture (Instruction Unit, Pipeline Schedulers, Scoreboarding over a GPU pool) is followed by two independent zooms, an instruction-to-DAG translation and a three-table scoreboard schema, the archetypal overview-plus-unlike-details split.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Let one architecture panel own the palette (gray boundaries, busy-slot shading) and name every subsystem directly on it, then let each detail panel use its own visual language, a dependency DAG with curved orange edges, a table with bracketed column groups in dark-red italics; keep font size well above this figure's dense, small-print floor.

exemplars.why_chosen: A single frame ties one packet's hardware pipeline to annotated P4 source code, a Cores diagram, and a Memory hierarchy via labelled C1, C2, Cb arrows, mixing code, diagram, and memory layout under one architecture.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Link annotated source-code lines to the specific execution units running them with small labelled arrows (C1, C2, Cb), and share one Memory box with explicit R, W, R&W arrows across foreground and background cores; strengthen the loose visual link this figure leaves between its top pipeline row and bottom detail row.

exemplars.why_chosen: Circled steps 1-8 walk a generic Traffic Manager pipeline (a), its cell-memory layout (b), then Themis's own hierarchical-bitmap scheduler with dual SRAM and HBM controllers (c), a zoom from generic module to the paper's extension.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Place the generic subsystem (a) and its generic memory layout (b) beside the paper's own scheduler (c) in one palette so the reader sees how little new logic Themis adds, and keep one inside legend (red data path, green dashed control path) for all three panels; avoid this figure's dense 4-5pt text.

exemplars.why_chosen: JBOF (a) and SSD-controller (b) architecture overviews sit beside a numbered 1-7 NVMe I/O-path zoom (c), a dense, 25-component, three-panel teardown of the traditional baseline system Espresso is built to replace.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Number every hop of one request, ring doorbell, fetch, parse and slice, address translation, DMA, flash command, directly on its connecting arrows to turn a static three-panel architecture into a traceable walkthrough; watch the density, 135 text labels and 310 shapes across three panels, a listed weakness.

exemplars.why_chosen: Panel (a)'s legend (orange control-header, green data-payload, blue network traffic) traces flows through one concrete 2-CPU, 8-GPU server, while panel (b) switches vocabulary entirely to TX, RX, Pacer engine threads and per-connection queue pairs.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw a layered software stack directly above the physical server hardware it runs on so flows can be colour-coded end to end (orange control, green data, blue network), and repeat that legend in the internal threading panel too, since this figure leaves it unstated there, a listed weakness.

exemplars.why_chosen: Kept after review although the note-writer judged the fit loose: one ungrouped panel of background small multiples, a generic Transformer block plus two quantization schemes plus two execution strategies, no lettered sub-panels, no dominant architecture view, explaining prior concepts, not the paper's own system.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Reserve composite-figure for a dominant architecture plus lettered unlike-kind detail panels; a flat, unlettered sequence of small background-concept diagrams like this one (Transformer block, then quantization, then execution strategy) is closer to small multiples and needs no single anchor panel, only consistent bit-width labels and dashed cross-reference arrows tying each stage to the next.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from composite-figure by the note-writer: both panels are sequential stages of one planning algorithm, template generation then plan instantiation, sharing one grayscale grid-of-squares glyph as a running anchor; that is two-panel's two-stages-of-one-thing case, not composite-figure's mix of unlike kinds.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Reuse one consistent glyph, here a grid of light/medium/dark squares sized by node count, across every panel of a multi-stage algorithm figure so a template's identity carries from generation through instantiation to the best-plan output; that continuity is a two-panel technique, not a reason to fragment into unlike-kind composite panels.

exemplars.why_chosen: Three unlike panels share one figure: an edge-cloud topology (a), two structurally identical but reorder-conflicting five-module NF chains stacked to expose the conflict (b), and a four-pipeline gateway ASIC (c) with 17 flows total.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack two structurally parallel chains directly above each other so a swapped module position jumps out without annotation; but unify panel styles with one shared palette, since packing an edge topology, chain diagrams and an ASIC block diagram with no common visual language is this figure's own listed weakness.

exemplars.why_chosen: Two framed chassis photos (24-bay front, 12-port back) sit beside a fully labelled internal diagram of one switch fanning into two identical 12-SSD pipelines, at nesting depth 5, the deepest figure in this set.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Frame a chassis photo with a thin border so it reads as one panel, not decoration, and reserve the fullest label depth (nesting depth 5 here) for the paper's own dual-pipeline internal view; avoid this figure's own weakness of collapsing 24 SSDs to bare ellipses with only a few labelled.

exemplars.why_chosen: Ranked first among mirrored-pair exemplars: client and proxy DChannel agents sit at the ends of five network swimlanes, each holding the same Packet steerer/Reordering buffer pair, mirrored in order, around the two crossing HBC/LLC channels.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Place the mirrored pair at the two ends of a swimlane network path rather than side by side, reverse the internal stacking order on the far side (steerer-then-buffer becomes buffer-then-steerer) to mirror it visually, and label the two crossing channel arrows in the figure itself, since no legend explains HBC and LLC here.

exemplars.why_chosen: Compute Node and Memory Node mirror the same Network Interface and Ethernet PHY P0/P1 stack, differing only in Application versus DDR4 controller, while the Switch sits on the axis between them carrying the EDM Scheduler.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Give the two mirrored peers different header colours when their roles genuinely differ, Application side versus DDR4 side, but keep every internal box (Network Interface, Ethernet PHY, matching port labels P0/P1) identically shaped and placed, and route the physical cabling as coloured arrows through the middle switch box that both sides share.

exemplars.why_chosen: Intel and Arm compute-node domains mirror the same Private Cache, Local Directory, Global CC/LLC stack, in red and purple, joined by a dashed CXL Bridges band to one shared, gold CXL Memory Expander Node above.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Give two heterogeneous host domains the identical internal box sequence (private caches, local directory, coherence block) so they read as one mirrored stack, then draw the shared directory they both bridge into as the one gold-accented box on the axis, and number the request and response arrows in one round trip out and back.

exemplars.why_chosen: Two full stacks, Graph Store Server then Worker Machine, mirror left and right at high confidence, with explicitly labelled Cross-Partition Communication and Parameter Synchronization arrows crossing the gap between the twin pairs.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack two double-column mirrored pairs vertically, storage servers over worker machines, keep each pair's internal boxes (Graph Store plus Samplers, Feature Cache Engine plus GPU Workers) identically arranged on both sides, and write the exact noun each crossing arrow carries, Cross-Partition Communication, Parameter Synchronization, directly on the arrow instead of leaving it implicit.

exemplars.why_chosen: Two Worker Node containers mirror the same Scheduler/Executors/Object Store stack, cross-connected to each other's object store and to redundant Coordinators above via a crossing X of arrows, over one wide Durable Key-Value Store.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw a crossing X of bidirectional arrows between a redundant top layer and the two mirrored containers below to show any-to-any reachability, keep each container's role colours (scheduler green, executor yellow, store light blue) identical on both sides, and let one wide shared-store box at the bottom serve as the axis of symmetry.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from mirrored-pair by the note-writer: four identically styled NN-defined modulator boxes (STF, LTF, SIG, DATA) run in parallel and converge into one Concatenate box, a four-way replicated-grid fan-in, not a two-peer mirrored pair.
exemplars.what_to_learn: The transferable move is replicated-grid's: draw every parallel member with identical size and fill so the reader reads them as interchangeable instances of one type, route each input to its member with a distinctly coloured dashed line, then converge all outputs into a single named merge box.

exemplars.why_chosen: The bottom half draws two Node boxes as identical Ingress-gateway/Pod, Virtual-switch, NIC stacks, linked by orange inter-node and yellow intra-node paths labelled Path 1 and Path 2, the double-column full-stack variant.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack each mirrored side as gateway/pod over virtual switch over NIC, and colour the two kinds of crossing path differently, orange for inter-node, yellow for intra-node, so a reader sees at a glance which path a request re-traverses the network stack; keep the busy per-pod annotations and legend from crowding the main stack shape.

exemplars.why_chosen: Prefill Instance and Decoding Instance stacks, each a pool of offset LLM Model/GPU/Parallel Runtime boxes, mirror left and right, joined by one labelled KV Cache Transfer arrow, with a shared Controller dispatching to both above.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw a pool of same-role instances as a small stack of offset boxes rather than one box, name the two mirrored pools by role (Prefill, Decoding) not by number, and put the one operation that crosses between them, KV Cache Transfer, on a single labelled arrow bridging the gap.

exemplars.why_chosen: VM1's red Page-Out path (steps 0-2) and VM2's slate Map-In path (steps 3-4) mirror around one shared HPA box, the same physical page moving from one VM's ownership to the other's.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Mirror two sides as a reclaim sequence and its inverse remap sequence, both numbered and both meeting at one shared physical-resource box in the centre, so the figure argues reuse rather than copying; add a second colour cue beyond red/slate, since only one accent colour marks the highlighted VM path here.

exemplars.why_chosen: Two full PGD-PUD-PMD-PTE table chains stack top (real, read-write) and bottom (CR3-rooted shadow, read-only), aligned column by column with vertical sync arrows crossing the dashed midline that is JANUS's actual integrity boundary.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Stack two identical multi-level structures, real above and shadow below, aligned column by column so vertical arrows can show exactly which levels sync and which do not, and mark the read-write versus read-only halves on either side of a single dashed midline instead of a caption note.

exemplars.why_chosen: The central Near-Storage Location, hosting the LVI Server, sits on the axis between two identical Near-User Location panels, each running the same Function Execution/Storage Library/Cache stack, the textbook central-server-flanked-by-two-instances case.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Flank one central server box with two literally identical copies of the peer panel, mirrored left and right, and route each peer's request/response arrows to the same handler inside the centre box; add colour or distinct line styles to the many double-headed arrows, since this exemplar uses none and they become hard to trace.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from mirrored-pair by the note-writer: three side-by-side CVM boxes (CVM1, CVM2, CVM3) roll up into one Server table below, a three-member replicated-grid aggregation, not two peers mirrored around a shared middle.
exemplars.what_to_learn: The transferable move is replicated-grid's: draw the same guaranteed-versus-oversubscribed split bar on every member, call out just one member's split in detail, then roll all members into one aggregate table below with the shared, scarce resource highlighted in its own colour, yellow for the oversubscribed pool here.

exemplars.why_chosen: Sender and Receiver cores mirror the same Processor Core/Program Code/Local Apic boxes either side of a shared UPID memory box, with seven numbered steps tracing one posted interrupt across the System Bus to EOI.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Put the one shared resource, here a UPID memory box, directly on the axis between two mirrored processor-core stacks, and number every step of a round trip 1 through 7 straight onto the arrows; disambiguate duplicate box labels (Processor Core, Program Code) with a Sender/Receiver header above each side rather than relabeling the boxes themselves.

exemplars.why_chosen: Memory Mode and Compute Mode panels mirror the identical Driver plus Memory-circuits grid, differing only in which GIA/GIAb/IA signals are active, meeting at the green Change Driver INPUT block that is the actual mode switch.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Use a mirrored pair to show one device in two operating modes, not just two devices: draw the exact same internal grid twice, side by side, and let one small accent-coloured block between them carry all the labelled signals that actually change between modes.

exemplars.why_chosen: Grace Encoder's and Grace Decoder's chains mirror each other left and right around one small coded-tensor icon at the centre, with a shared orange/blue NN-vs-non-NN legend applied identically to both sides.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Mirror an encoder and decoder around one small icon standing in for the data actually transmitted between them, and apply one binary colour legend, orange for learned modules, blue for classical ones, to both chains identically so a reader sees at a glance how much of the traditional codec structure survives.

exemplars.why_chosen: Client and Server run the same HTTP/QUIC/UDP base stack with only their role-specific additions differing, Tunnel wrapping versus rate-control modules, while the Tunnel Server's three named modules occupy the shared middle carrying TECC's contribution.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Keep the common base protocol stack identical on both end nodes and add only the role-specific boxes where the design differs, client-side tunnel wrapping, server-side rate control, then dedicate the entire middle box to the paper's own contribution with named sub-modules. Disambiguate repeated HTTP/QUIC/UDP labels by column position, since duplicates can confuse a fast reader.

exemplars.why_chosen: Sender and Receiver diagrams mirror the same VMs-over-CIPU-Hardware-Accelerator-over-Software stack with swapped internal box order, and nine circled numbers keyed to a shared middle legend trace one spray-reorder-ACK round trip across both.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Swap the internal stacking order of the mirrored receiver relative to the sender, hardware-then-software becomes software-then-hardware, so the eye still reads top-to-bottom as protocol flow on both sides, and key every circled step number to one shared legend panel placed between the two mirrored diagrams rather than beside either one.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from flanked-core by the note-writer: three matched four-layer stacks (Compute Node, Switch, Memory Node) sit side by side, with the paper's Central Scheduler contribution accent-filled on the switch axis between two mirrored sides, not a core flanked by bands.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Align identical protocol-stack layers across parallel columns so a reader compares row by row, and put the paper's actual contribution (the scheduler) on the shared axis between the two mirrored sides, accent-filled, rather than folding it into a bottom hardware band.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star, medium-confidence two-band variant: a User/Kernel line sits above the Manager core, which nests four submodules across 9 components, handing off to a Scheduler/Monitor pair as the band below.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Put the privilege boundary between the caller band and the core rather than lower down, give the core four labelled submodules so it reads as an engine, and let two kernel-side modules share the band below as equals instead of nesting one inside the other.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence, star-ranked (3rd) reading of a GPU training core fed by three circled, numbered noise sources, each cross-referenced against a three-item legend pill-stack labelled Distributed Noise History on the right.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When several distributed hardware sources all feed one engine box, number each source and give it a matching entry in a compact legend column instead of writing the source name on every arrow; keep the engine's internal stages in a dashed sub-box like the DP Training region here.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star, rank-4, high-confidence 15-component exemplar: Request/Response Queues flank the Offline Profiler and Plan Optimizer as a small core, itself sandwiched between an HTTP-server interface band above and a GPU-Pool-bearing Worker Node band below.
exemplars.what_to_learn: The flanked-core sandwich can nest inside a larger layered stack: draw the two queues as small pills on either side of the planning core rather than as generic arrows, and give the bottom hardware band its own internal grid of managers instead of a single box.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star, rank-6 canonical exemplar: five circled numbers trace a path through the Skyloft LibOS core, a Scheduling Policy pill-stack sits beside it, and a dotted line marks the user/kernel boundary above the hardware band.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Run a numbered path through the core's internal submodules and draw interchangeable scheduling policies as a stack of index-card pills beside it; but number branches only when they truly form one sequence; here steps 2/3 split from the scheduler while 4/5 arrive independently from hardware, so the numbering reads as separate paths, not one flow.

exemplars.why_chosen: Medium-confidence, rank-7 exemplar of the horizontal variant: a formally verified container V sits between untrusted peers A and B, all three resting above the microkernel's endpoint data structures in the band below.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Flank the trusted middle component with its untrusted peers in one row rather than stacking all three, and match send()/recv() call labels on the two boxes that actually interact; the weakness here is that the third peer is drawn but never wired to anything, so give every peer at least one visible arrow.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star, high-confidence textbook case, 22 components: a purple KTransformers core sits between a tan User Interface band above and a tan Heterogeneous Hardware band below, with MoE Models and Advanced Operators as pill-stack side columns.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Use large white block arrows on all four sides to funnel bands and side columns into the core, keep both side columns as plain stacked pills naming interchangeable models or kernels, and show the core's own transformation as a small before/after computation-graph icon rather than prose.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star, rank-9 exemplar: a teal Request Scheduler core nesting three submodules sits above a shared GPU worker pool as the hardware band, with a purple Global Monitor as a side column closing the allocation loop.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Put the routing decision box above the shared resource pool it feeds and give the side monitor its own feedback arrow back into that pool rather than into the core; the weakness here is too many small labelled arrows crowd the scheduler, so budget space for routing labels before adding a monitor loop.

exemplars.why_chosen: Medium-confidence, 11-component exemplar: a Host band of four send-queue boxes sits above the RNIC band, inside which an Event Mux core with four submodules (QPC, Schedule Policy, Schedule Queue) aggregates doorbell, credit and dequeue signals.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Place the caller band's repeated small boxes (four send queues here) in one row above the hardware band, then let a single mux-shaped core inside that band collect every event type by arrow direction alone rather than colour, so in and out of the core reads as the only code that matters.

exemplars.why_chosen: Medium-confidence context figure: a red-outlined Granular Task Scheduler core sits below three Application boxes and beside a stacked Spark/MapReduce Scheduler side column, both feeding a Rack-Server-and-Worker-Pool hardware band at the bottom.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Outline the paper's own contribution in a single accent colour against a gray-and-white field of existing infrastructure, and stack the interchangeable pre-existing schedulers as a plain side column beside it; the weakness here is a uniform tiny font across many labels, so give the emphasized box more visual weight, not just an outline.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star, rank-14, dense 14-component exemplar: a stacked-paper Programs band on top feeds a Process Table side column into an LLM Engine core nesting five submodules (Priority Function, Scheduler, Memory Manager, KV Cache, Model Executor).
exemplars.what_to_learn: Use a stacked-paper icon behind a box to signal many concurrent instances without drawing them all, and route shared metadata into both the dispatcher and the engine's scheduler; the weakness is that the long wraparound arrow carrying it into the engine is easy to miss, so keep shared-state arrows short and direct.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star, rank-15 textbook fit: three Application boxes form the interface band, a nested Cortex core sits below, and a dashed Region-A/B line marks the trust boundary above the Remote Data Service band of three pills.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Put the trust or region boundary as a dashed line directly between the core and the bottom band, exactly where the rule calls for it, and draw that bottom band as a row of three named service pills rather than one generic box; number the steps so cache-hit and cache-miss paths both stay traceable.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star, rank-16 exemplar at only 5 components: two Trustlet peers flank an Object core marked with a red X, all resting on a Trusted Monitor band, a trusted-middle pattern at half the usual component count.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Mark a denied access path with one bold red X on the shared object rather than a caption, and give the figure a small top-right legend distinguishing solid data-path arrows from dashed control-path arrows; the weakness here is that the X itself has no legend entry, so give every ad hoc symbol one too.

exemplars.why_chosen: High-confidence, 13-component exemplar with a numbered 7-step path through the Conveyor Core hub, flanked by two dashed pill-columns of interchangeable plug-ins, Artifact Finders on one side and Action Services on the other.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Draw each side column as a dashed group box containing named interchangeable plug-ins (finders, action services) rather than one generic label, and number the full request path across both wings so a reader can follow create-then-run without a separate legend; add a legend anyway once box types multiply beyond dashed-versus-solid.

exemplars.why_chosen: Star, 25-component exemplar: inside the purple Hydro Coordinator band, a Cluster Scheduler core sits flanked left by two allocator boxes and right by an Elastic Executor, a flanked-core micro-pattern nested inside a layered whole.
exemplars.what_to_learn: A flanked-core sandwich can appear at any scale: repeat the same left-core-right composition inside one band of a larger layered figure, colour that band and its neighbour differently, and orange-highlight the technique sub-boxes inside each; the weakness here is the central box's role is legible only from position, so add one line to it.

exemplars.why_chosen: Doc-cited exemplar of the two-small-hubs variant: GKBuilder and GKProbe sit as paired hubs inside the VMM band, mediating a Target/Observer pair above the Hypervisor's EPT pill band, plus a lettered key and numbered path.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Colour-code new components differently from the existing infrastructure they sit inside (white boxes on a grey VMM here) and give the bottom hardware band its own row of small pills; the weakness is that overlaying a lettered key and a numbered step sequence on one figure slows parsing, so pick one scheme per diagram.

exemplars.why_chosen: Medium-confidence, 14-component microarchitecture instance of the pattern: a Data-plane core with six sub-blocks sits between top bus-address pills and a bottom Control Plane band, flanked left and right by matching Register File Interface columns.
exemplars.what_to_learn: The flanked-core sandwich also works for on-chip blocks: use bus-width labels on the connecting lines instead of arrows, and colour every block by whether it scales with datapath width so the tunable parameter is visible at a glance; the weakness is that wiring beyond bus widths stays unlabelled, so name the bus's purpose too.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from flanked-core by the note-writer: a 19-component, 14-flow left-to-right compiler pipeline (LLVM to DSL to E-graph) runs through one boxed iterative Phase loop and out to HLS-synthesized instructions, a pipeline with a loop, not an engine between bands.
exemplars.what_to_learn: Box one iterative loop (equality saturation, anti-unification, vectorization, selection) inside a highlighted sub-region of a longer pipeline rather than drawing every pass as a separate top-level stage; the weakness here is that those sub-step boxes carry only short keywords, so a reader needs the matching subsection to interpret them.

exemplars.why_chosen: Reassigned from flanked-core by the note-writer: three co-equal dashed bands (Applications, LinkLab Edge/Cloud Runtime, KubeEdge) stack bottom-up with zero arrows, pure vertical containment standing for 'runs on top of', not one core distinguished from its bands.
exemplars.what_to_learn: When a stack has no data flow to show, drop the arrows entirely and let vertical position alone mean 'runs on top of', colouring only the layer that is the paper's own contribution against reused third-party logos elsewhere; this is a layered stack, so do not force a middle tier into a flanked-core engine role.
